prompt: A clinic records systolic blood pressure for the same 25 patients before and after an 8-week exercise program. The 25 before-minus-after differences are roughly normal. The analyst wants to test whether mean blood pressure changed. Which test is most appropriate?

options.text: A two-sample t-test with unequal variances (Welch's t-test)
A chi-squared test of independence on the two sets of readings
A one-way ANOVA treating before and after as two groups
A paired t-test on the before-and-after differences

explanation: The readings are two measurements on the same patients, so a paired t-test on the per-patient differences is correct and removes between-patient variation. Welch's t-test and a one-way ANOVA both assume the two groups are independent samples, which they are not. A chi-squared test of independence works on counts of categorical variables, not on continuous measurements.

prompt: An analyst has these customer counts by region and preferred plan. North: Basic 120, Premium 80. South: Basic 90, Premium 110. The question is whether plan preference is associated with region. Which test should be used?

options.text: A Pearson correlation between region and plan
A paired t-test comparing the North and South counts
A one-way ANOVA comparing the number of customers in each plan by region
A chi-squared test of independence on the 2x2 contingency table

explanation: Both variables are categorical and the data are counts in a contingency table, which is exactly what a chi-squared test of independence evaluates. A Pearson correlation measures linear association between two continuous variables. A paired t-test compares means of paired continuous measurements. A one-way ANOVA compares means of a continuous outcome across groups, and there is no continuous outcome here.

prompt: An analyst compares average order value across four store layouts with a one-way ANOVA. The output is: F = 5.8, df = (3, 196), p = 0.001. Which conclusion and next step are correct?

options.text: All four layout means differ from each other, so no further testing is needed
At least one layout mean differs; run a post hoc test such as Tukey's HSD to find which
The four layouts have unequal variances, so the analysis should switch to a chi-squared test
Store layout explains 58 percent of the variance in order value

explanation: A significant ANOVA F statistic says only that the group means are not all equal; a post hoc procedure such as Tukey's HSD identifies which pairs differ while controlling the family-wise error rate. It does not show that every pair differs. The F statistic is a ratio of between-group to within-group variance, not a test of unequal variances and not a percentage of variance explained (that would be eta-squared).

prompt: A churn classifier is evaluated on 1,000 customers with these results: TP = 60, FP = 20, FN = 40, TN = 880. Which set of metrics is correct for the churn class?

options.text: Precision 0.60, recall 0.75, F1 0.67
Precision 0.75, recall 0.98, F1 0.85
Precision 0.75, recall 0.60, F1 0.45
Precision 0.75, recall 0.60, F1 0.67

explanation: Precision is TP/(TP+FP) = 60/80 = 0.75, recall is TP/(TP+FN) = 60/100 = 0.60, and F1 is their harmonic mean, 2(0.75)(0.60)/(1.35) = 0.67. Precision 0.60 with recall 0.75 swaps the two formulas. A recall of 0.98 is actually specificity, TN/(TN+FP) = 880/900. An F1 of 0.45 is the product of precision and recall, not the harmonic mean.

prompt: A defect detector is tested on 10,000 parts, of which 100 are defective. Model A flags no parts at all. Model B gives TP = 80, FN = 20, FP = 120, TN = 9,780. A manager points out that Model A has the higher accuracy. Which single metric uses all four confusion-matrix cells and would correctly rank Model B above Model A?

options.text: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)
Accuracy across all 10,000 parts
Specificity (true negative rate)
False positive rate on good parts

explanation: MCC combines TP, TN, FP and FN into a correlation between predicted and actual labels; Model A scores 0 (no skill) while Model B is clearly positive, so it stays informative under heavy class imbalance. Accuracy favours Model A (0.990 versus 0.986) because it rewards predicting the majority class. Specificity and the false positive rate use only the negative class, and Model A is perfect on both because it never flags anything.

prompt: A decision tree parent node has 100 samples and entropy 0.90. Two candidate splits are evaluated. Split A: child 1 has 40 samples with entropy 0.50, child 2 has 60 samples with entropy 0.60. Split B: child 1 has 50 samples with entropy 0.20, child 2 has 50 samples with entropy 0.80. Which split should the tree choose using information gain?

options.text: Split A, with an information gain of 0.34
Split B, with an information gain of 0.40
Split B, with an information gain of 0.50
Split A, with an information gain of 0.56

explanation: Information gain is the parent entropy minus the size-weighted child entropy. For Split A the weighted entropy is 0.4(0.50) + 0.6(0.60) = 0.56, a gain of 0.34; for Split B it is 0.5(0.20) + 0.5(0.80) = 0.50, a gain of 0.40, so Split B is chosen. The value 0.50 for Split B is its weighted child entropy, not the gain, and 0.56 is Split A's weighted child entropy.

prompt: A decision tree node contains 80 approved and 20 denied loan applications. What is the Gini impurity of this node?
explanation: Gini impurity is 1 minus the sum of squared class proportions: 1 - (0.8^2 + 0.2^2) = 1 - 0.68 = 0.32. The value 0.68 is the sum of squared proportions itself. The value 0.16 is the product 0.8 x 0.2, which is half the binary Gini. About 0.72 is the entropy of this node in bits, a different impurity measure.

prompt: A quality team lowers its significance level from 0.05 to 0.01 for a test of whether a new supplier's parts are weaker. The sample size and true effect size do not change. What happens to the error rates?

options.text: Both Type I and Type II errors become less likely
Type I errors become more likely and Type II errors become less likely
Type I errors become less likely and Type II errors become more likely
Neither error rate changes; only the reported p value changes

explanation: Alpha is the Type I error rate, so lowering it to 0.01 makes false rejections rarer, but the stricter threshold also makes real effects harder to detect, which lowers power and raises the Type II error rate. Both rates can fall together only by increasing sample size or effect size. Raising Type I errors would require a higher alpha. The p value depends on the data, not on alpha, and alpha directly sets the Type I error rate.

prompt: An A/B test of a new checkout page reports p = 0.03 for the difference in conversion rate, where the null hypothesis is no difference. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: There is a 3 percent probability that the null hypothesis of no difference is true
Assuming no true difference, a result this extreme would occur about 3 percent of the time
There is a 97 percent probability that the new page converts better than the old one
The new page improves the conversion rate by about 3 percentage points over the old one

explanation: A p value is the probability, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a result at least as extreme as the one seen. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and its complement is not the probability that the alternative is true; those statements need a Bayesian analysis with a prior. The p value also says nothing about the size of the effect.

prompt: A survey of 400 customers gives a 95 percent confidence interval for mean satisfaction with a margin of error of plus or minus 0.6 points. Leadership wants a margin of error of plus or minus 0.3 points at the same confidence level. Assuming the standard deviation stays the same, about how many customers are needed?
explanation: The margin of error is proportional to 1 divided by the square root of n, so halving it requires four times the sample: 4 x 400 = 1,600. Doubling the sample to 800 reduces the margin only by a factor of about 1.41, to roughly 0.42. A sample of 3,200 would cut the margin to about 0.21, more than required. A sample of 1,200 would give about 0.35, which is still too wide.

prompt: Two regression models predict monthly energy use for 200 buildings. Model A: 6 predictors, training R2 0.842, adjusted R2 0.837, holdout RMSE 10.2 kWh. Model B: 60 predictors, training R2 0.861, adjusted R2 0.801, holdout RMSE 12.7 kWh. Which model should be preferred?

options.text: Model B, because it has the higher training R2
Model B, because adding predictors always reduces holdout RMSE
Model A, because Model B's extra predictors lower adjusted R2 and raise holdout error
Neither, because an R2 below 0.90 means a regression model is not usable for decisions

explanation: Adjusted R2 penalises predictors that do not improve fit enough to justify them, and Model B's adjusted R2 drops to 0.801 while its holdout RMSE rises, the signature of overfitting. Training R2 never decreases when predictors are added, so it cannot be used to compare models of different sizes. Extra predictors often increase holdout error by adding variance. There is no universal R2 threshold for usability; it depends on the problem.

prompt: A data scientist fits three count models to 5,000 records. Model A has 3 parameters and AIC 1520.4. Model B has 6 parameters and AIC 1498.2. Model C has 12 parameters and AIC 1502.9. Which model should be selected?

options.text: Model A, because AIC always favours the model with the fewest parameters
Model C, because the model with the most parameters always fits best
Model B, because it has the lowest AIC
Model A, because a higher AIC indicates a better fit

explanation: AIC trades off fit against complexity, and the model with the lowest AIC is preferred, which is Model B. AIC does not simply favour the fewest parameters; Model A's poorer fit outweighs its smaller penalty. Model C may fit the training data slightly better, but its extra parameters are not worth the penalty. Higher AIC means worse, not better. With n = 5,000, BIC (penalty k ln n) would penalise Model C's parameters even more heavily.

prompt: For 300 support agents, monthly tickets resolved rises steeply with tenure in the first two years and then levels off, but never decreases. A few agents have extreme ticket counts. Which measure best captures the strength of association between tenure and tickets resolved?

options.text: Spearman rank correlation
Pearson correlation coefficient
R2 from a straight-line fit of tickets on tenure
Point-biserial correlation

explanation: Spearman correlation works on ranks, so it measures how consistently one variable increases with the other (a monotonic relationship) and is resistant to extreme values. Pearson correlation measures only linear association and is pulled by outliers. R2 from a straight-line fit is the square of the Pearson correlation and has the same weaknesses. Point-biserial correlation is for one binary and one continuous variable.

prompt: On a validation set, a newly built classifier has a ROC AUC of 0.20. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is slightly better than random, because any AUC above zero indicates some skill
Its scores are systematically inverted; reversing them would give an AUC of 0.80
It has 20 percent accuracy at the default threshold of 0.5
It is worse than random and contains no usable information

explanation: AUC is the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative; 0.20 means negatives are usually scored higher, so the ranking is informative but backwards, often because of a label or sign error, and 1 - 0.20 = 0.80. Random ranking gives 0.50, so 0.20 is not better than random as scored. AUC is threshold-free and is not an accuracy figure. Calling it useless ignores the strong, inverted signal.

prompt: A data scientist repeatedly draws samples of 100 transaction amounts from a strongly right-skewed population and records each sample mean. Which statement correctly describes the collection of sample means?

options.text: The individual transaction amounts become normal as more samples are drawn
The sample means keep the same right skew as the raw transaction amounts
The sample means are approximately normal and centred on the population mean
Each sample mean equals the population mean exactly, by the law of large numbers

explanation: The central limit theorem says the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows, whatever the shape of the population (given finite variance), centred on the population mean. The raw amounts keep their skewed distribution no matter how many samples are drawn. The skew of the sample means shrinks as n grows. The law of large numbers says sample means converge toward the population mean as n increases, not that any single sample mean equals it.

prompt: Which distributions best model these three variables? (1) The number of customers, out of 20 contacted, who accept an offer, each with the same acceptance probability. (2) The number of server errors logged per hour at a constant average rate. (3) A start time chosen with equal likelihood anywhere in a 60-minute window.

options.text: (1) Poisson, (2) binomial, (3) uniform
(1) Binomial, (2) normal, (3) Poisson
(1) Normal, (2) Poisson, (3) power law
(1) Binomial, (2) Poisson, (3) uniform

explanation: A fixed number of independent trials with a constant success probability gives a binomial count. Events occurring independently at a constant average rate per interval give a Poisson count. Equal likelihood over a fixed interval is a continuous uniform distribution. Swapping binomial and Poisson ignores that (1) has a fixed upper limit of 20 and (2) does not. A normal distribution is continuous and a poor default for small counts, and a power law describes heavy-tailed quantities, not an equal-likelihood window.

prompt: An analyst has 12 measurements of a chemical process yield and needs a 95 percent confidence interval for the mean. The population standard deviation is unknown. Which distribution should provide the critical value?

options.text: The standard normal distribution, using the sample standard deviation
A t distribution with 11 degrees of freedom
A t distribution with 12 degrees of freedom
A chi-squared distribution with 11 degrees of freedom

explanation: When the standard deviation is estimated from a small sample, the standardized mean follows a t distribution with n - 1 = 11 degrees of freedom, whose heavier tails widen the interval to reflect the extra uncertainty. Using the standard normal understates that uncertainty for n = 12. Using 12 degrees of freedom forgets that one degree of freedom is used to estimate the mean. The chi-squared distribution is used for intervals on a variance, not a mean.

prompt: On log-log axes, the number of accounts plotted against follower count falls on a roughly straight line with negative slope, and a handful of accounts have millions of followers. What does this suggest?

options.text: A normal distribution, so about 95 percent of accounts lie within two standard deviations
An exponential distribution, because exponentials are straight lines on log-log axes
A power-law distribution, so the sample mean is unstable and dominated by extreme values
A uniform distribution, because the points lie on a straight line

explanation: A straight line on log-log axes is the signature of a power law, whose heavy tail means a few huge values dominate the mean and variance, so medians or quantiles summarise it better. A normal distribution has thin tails and would not produce accounts millions of times larger than typical. An exponential distribution is a straight line on a semi-log plot (log y against linear x), not on log-log axes. A uniform distribution would show constant frequency.

prompt: A summary of insurance claim amounts shows: mean 4,800, median 2,100, skewness 3.2, excess kurtosis 14. Which two conclusions are supported?

options.text: The distribution is left-skewed because the median is below the mean
The claims are approximately normal because the kurtosis is positive
The distribution has a long right tail
The median is a poorer summary of a typical claim than the mean
Extreme claims occur far more often than a normal distribution would predict

explanation: Positive skewness and a mean well above the median both indicate a long right tail, and a large positive excess kurtosis means heavier tails than a normal distribution, so extreme claims are much more common. A median below the mean indicates right skew, not left skew. A normal distribution has excess kurtosis of zero, so 14 is far from normal. In a heavily right-skewed distribution the median is the better summary of a typical value, because the mean is pulled up by the tail.

prompt: In a regression of household spending on income, the residuals spread out more and more as income increases. What is this, and what is its main consequence for ordinary least squares?

options.text: Homoskedasticity; the usual OLS standard errors and p values remain valid as reported
Heteroskedasticity; coefficients stay unbiased but standard errors and p values are unreliable
Heteroskedasticity; the coefficient estimates become biased toward zero and inconsistent as n grows
Multicollinearity; the coefficients become unstable and change sign across samples

explanation: Non-constant residual variance is heteroskedasticity. OLS coefficients remain unbiased, but the usual standard errors assume constant variance, so confidence intervals and p values are wrong; robust standard errors, weighted least squares or a transformation address it. Homoskedasticity means constant variance, the opposite of what is described. Heteroskedasticity does not by itself bias the coefficients. Multicollinearity concerns correlated predictors, not the pattern of residual spread.

prompt: Delivery time X in days has this cumulative distribution function: F(2) = 0.30, F(5) = 0.75, F(7) = 0.95. What is the probability that a delivery takes more than 2 days but no more than 5 days?
explanation: The CDF gives P(X <= x), so P(2 < X <= 5) = F(5) - F(2) = 0.75 - 0.30 = 0.45. The value 0.75 is P(X <= 5), which includes deliveries of 2 days or less. The value 0.30 is P(X <= 2). The value 0.25 is P(X > 5). For a continuous variable the same probability is the area under the probability density function between 2 and 5; for a discrete one it is the sum of the probability mass function over that range.

prompt: Readings from a sensor are normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 4. Approximately what percentage of readings exceed 58?

options.text: 5 percent
16 percent
2.5 percent
0.15 percent

explanation: A reading of 58 is (58 - 50)/4 = 2 standard deviations above the mean. About 95 percent of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations, leaving about 5 percent split equally between the two tails, so about 2.5 percent exceed 58. The figure 5 percent counts both tails. About 16 percent lies above 1 standard deviation. About 0.15 percent lies above 3 standard deviations.

prompt: A fraud model flags 90 percent of fraudulent transactions and wrongly flags 10 percent of legitimate transactions. In the population being scored, 10 percent of transactions are fraudulent. If a transaction is flagged, what is the probability that it is actually fraudulent?

options.text: 90 percent
10 percent
81 percent
50 percent

explanation: By Bayes' rule, out of 1,000 transactions 100 are fraudulent and 90 of them are flagged, while 900 are legitimate and 90 of them are flagged. Of the 180 flagged, 90 are fraud, so P(fraud | flagged) = 0.5. The 90 percent figure is the sensitivity, P(flagged | fraud), which is a different conditional probability. The 10 percent figure is the base rate before any evidence. The 81 percent figure has no basis in the calculation.

prompt: A promotion has a 20 percent chance of producing a $5,000 gain and an 80 percent chance of producing a $1,000 loss. What is the expected value of running the promotion?

options.text: A gain of $200
A gain of $4,000
A gain of $2,000
A gain of $1,000

explanation: Expected value is the probability-weighted sum of outcomes: 0.2 x 5,000 + 0.8 x (-1,000) = 1,000 - 800 = 200. The $4,000 figure adds the two outcomes without weighting them. The $2,000 figure is the simple average of the two outcomes, which treats them as equally likely. The $1,000 figure counts only the weighted gain and ignores the expected loss.

prompt: A project has five sequential tasks. For each task, the team can give only a minimum and maximum duration, and any value in between is considered equally likely. Management wants the probability that the project finishes within 40 days. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Add the midpoints of the five ranges and compare the total expected duration with the 40-day deadline
Monte Carlo simulation: sample each task from its range, sum, repeat many times, count runs within 40 days
Bootstrap the five range endpoints and take the median of the resampled project totals
Add the five maximum durations and report the project as late if that sum exceeds 40 days

explanation: Monte Carlo simulation samples the uncertain inputs from their distributions many times and builds the distribution of the total, from which the proportion of runs at or under 40 days estimates the probability. Summing midpoints gives a single expected total but no probability. Bootstrapping resamples observed data, and five range endpoints are not a sample of project outcomes. Summing the maxima gives a worst case that is very unlikely, not a probability.

prompt: An analyst has 60 observations of equipment repair cost. The data are strongly skewed, and the analyst needs a 95 percent confidence interval for the median without assuming any particular distribution. Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Bootstrap: resample the 60 values with replacement and use percentiles of the resampled medians
Report the sample median plus or minus 1.96 sample standard deviations of the costs
Fit a normal distribution to the 60 costs and simulate many sample medians from that fitted model
Compute a t interval for the mean cost and report it as the interval for the median

explanation: The bootstrap approximates the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling the observed data with replacement, so it gives an interval for the median without distributional assumptions. Plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations describes the spread of individual values, not uncertainty in the median. Simulating from a fitted normal imposes an assumption the skewed data violate. A t interval for the mean answers a different question, and in skewed data the mean and median differ.

prompt: Classify the missingness in each case. (1) A logger's battery fails at random times, so some readings are lost. (2) Older patients, whose ages are recorded, are more likely to miss a follow-up visit. (3) Heavy drinkers are more likely to leave a question about alcohol consumption blank.

options.text: (1) MAR, (2) MCAR, (3) MNAR
(1) MCAR, (2) MNAR, (3) MAR
(1) MNAR, (2) MAR, (3) MCAR
(1) MCAR, (2) MAR, (3) MNAR

explanation: Missing completely at random (MCAR) means missingness is unrelated to any data, as with random battery failures. Missing at random (MAR) means missingness depends only on observed variables, here recorded age. Missing not at random (MNAR) means missingness depends on the unobserved value itself, here the amount of drinking. The other combinations misassign at least one case; for example, the follow-up case is not MNAR because the variable driving missingness, age, is observed.

prompt: A fraud data set has 200,000 transactions, of which 0.5 percent are fraud. The team will split the data 80/20 into training and test sets and wants both sets to have the same fraud rate. Which approach should be used?

options.text: A stratified split on the fraud label
A simple random split with a fixed random seed
Sorting by transaction amount and splitting at the 80th percentile
Oversampling fraud cases across the full data set before splitting

explanation: Stratified splitting samples within each class so that the training and test sets keep the original 0.5 percent fraud rate, which matters when the class is rare. A fixed seed makes a random split reproducible but does not guarantee the same class proportions. Splitting by amount puts systematically different transactions in each set. Oversampling before splitting copies minority records into both sets, leaking information and distorting the test set's class rate.

prompt: A national survey deliberately oversamples rural households so that rural estimates are precise. Rural households are 10 percent of the population but 30 percent of the sample. What must be done when estimating national averages?

options.text: Nothing, because a larger rural sample makes every national estimate more accurate without weights
Drop rural respondents at random until they make up 10 percent of the sample again
Average the rural and urban means with equal weight to get the national figure
Apply sampling weights that down-weight rural respondents by their higher selection probability

explanation: Oversampling a stratum changes selection probabilities, so national estimates need weights inversely proportional to each respondent's selection probability; otherwise rural answers are over-represented threefold. Leaving the data unweighted biases national figures toward rural values. Discarding respondents wastes data and reduces precision when weighting achieves the same correction. A simple mean of the two group averages treats rural and urban as equal halves of the population, which they are not.

prompt: A feature matrix X has 500 rows (observations) and 20 columns (features). A weight matrix W is 20 x 3. Which statement about the matrix products is correct?

options.text: XW is 20 x 3, and the transpose product X^T X is 500 x 500
XW is 500 x 3, and the transpose product X^T X is 20 x 20
WX is 3 x 500, and the transpose product X^T X is 20 x 20
XW is 500 x 3, and the transpose product X^T X is 500 x 500

explanation: A product AB is defined when A's column count equals B's row count, and the result takes A's rows and B's columns, so (500 x 20)(20 x 3) is 500 x 3. Transposing X gives 20 x 500, so X^T X is (20 x 500)(500 x 20) = 20 x 20. WX is undefined because W has 3 columns and X has 500 rows. A 500 x 500 result would come from X X^T, not X^T X.

prompt: A 1,000 x 6 design matrix contains an intercept column, temp_C, temp_F (where temp_F = 1.8 x temp_C + 32) and three other independent features. What is the rank of the matrix, and what is the consequence for ordinary least squares?

options.text: Rank 6; the constant 32 makes temp_F independent of temp_C
Rank 5; X^T X is singular, so the OLS coefficients have no unique solution
Rank 5; X^T X becomes invertible again once the columns are standardized
Rank 1,000; the rank equals the number of rows

explanation: temp_F is an exact linear combination of the intercept and temp_C, so only 5 columns are linearly independent and the rank is 5. With rank below the number of columns, X^T X is singular and infinitely many coefficient vectors fit equally well. Adding a constant is still a linear combination once an intercept column is present. Standardizing rescales columns but keeps the exact dependence. Rank cannot exceed the smaller dimension, here 6.

prompt: The covariance matrix of three features has eigenvalues 6, 3 and 1. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The total variance is 18, and the first principal component explains 33 percent of it
The total variance is 10, and the first principal component explains 6 percent of it
The total variance is 6, and the first principal component explains all of it
The total variance is 10, and the first principal component explains 60 percent of it

explanation: The trace of a covariance matrix equals the sum of its eigenvalues and equals the total variance, 6 + 3 + 1 = 10. Each eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector (principal component), so the first explains 6/10 = 60 percent. The product of the eigenvalues, 18, is the determinant, not the total variance. Six percent misplaces the decimal, and the largest eigenvalue alone is not the total variance.

prompt: An engineer fits a least squares model on a large, nearly collinear design by explicitly computing the inverse of X^T X. The coefficients change wildly with tiny changes in the data. Which approach gives a more numerically stable solution?

options.text: Multiply X^T X by the identity matrix before computing its inverse
Invert the transpose of X^T X instead of inverting X^T X itself
Solve the least squares problem with a QR or singular value decomposition
Round every feature to two decimal places before computing the inverse

explanation: Matrix decompositions such as QR or SVD solve least squares without forming and inverting X^T X, which squares the condition number and amplifies rounding error; SVD also exposes near-zero singular values that cause the instability. Multiplying by the identity matrix leaves a matrix unchanged, because I times A equals A. X^T X is symmetric, so its transpose is the same matrix. Rounding the inputs adds error and does not fix ill-conditioning.

prompt: A team compares support articles using TF-IDF vectors. Long articles have much larger term weights than short ones on the same topic, and the team wants similarity to reflect topic rather than length. Which measure should be used?

options.text: Cosine similarity
Euclidean distance
Manhattan distance
Hamming distance

explanation: Cosine similarity depends only on the angle between vectors, so two articles with the same term proportions score as similar regardless of length. Euclidean and Manhattan distances both grow with vector magnitude, so a long and a short article on the same topic look far apart. Hamming distance counts positions where values differ, which suits equal-length binary or categorical strings rather than continuous TF-IDF weights.

prompt: On a city grid where vehicles can travel only along streets running north-south and east-west, depot A is at (1, 2) and customer B is at (4, 6), in kilometres. What are the Euclidean and Manhattan distances between them, and which better approximates driving distance?

options.text: Euclidean 5 km, Manhattan 7 km; Manhattan better approximates driving distance
Euclidean 7 km, Manhattan 5 km; Euclidean better approximates driving distance
Euclidean 25 km, Manhattan 7 km; Manhattan better approximates driving distance
Euclidean 5 km, Manhattan 5 km; both approximate driving distance equally

explanation: The differences are 3 and 4, so Euclidean distance is the square root of (9 + 16) = 5 and Manhattan distance is 3 + 4 = 7. On a grid, travel follows the axes, which is what Manhattan distance measures. Swapping the values confuses the two formulas. The value 25 is the squared Euclidean distance. The two distances are equal only when the points share a coordinate.

prompt: A support vector machine with a linear kernel underfits a data set in which one class forms a ring around the other. Which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the linear kernel and increase the penalty parameter C to reduce training errors
Switch to a polynomial kernel of degree 1 to add flexibility to the decision boundary
Use a cosine similarity kernel so that the length of each vector is ignored
Switch to a radial basis function kernel, whose similarity decays with squared distance

explanation: The radial basis function (RBF) kernel measures similarity as exp(-gamma x squared Euclidean distance), an exponential that decays with distance, which lets the SVM form curved, closed boundaries such as a circle around the inner class. A linear kernel can draw only a straight boundary, so raising C just penalises errors more without changing the boundary's shape. A degree-1 polynomial kernel is linear. A cosine kernel compares directions from the origin, which does not separate a ring from its centre.

prompt: A loss function is L(w1, w2) = w1^2 + 3 w1 w2 + w2^2. What is the gradient of L at (w1, w2) = (1, 2)?
explanation: The partial derivatives are dL/dw1 = 2 w1 + 3 w2 = 2 + 6 = 8 and dL/dw2 = 3 w1 + 2 w2 = 3 + 4 = 7, so the gradient is (8, 7). Reversing the components assigns each partial to the wrong parameter. The vector (2, 4) keeps only the squared terms and ignores the cross term 3 w1 w2. The value 11 is the loss itself at that point, 1 + 6 + 4, not a derivative.

prompt: A single neuron computes z = w x + b and y_hat = sigmoid(z). During back propagation, dL/dy_hat = 0.5, dy_hat/dz = 0.2 and the input x = 3. What is dL/dw?
explanation: By the chain rule, dL/dw = dL/dy_hat x dy_hat/dz x dz/dw, and dz/dw = x, so the result is 0.5 x 0.2 x 3 = 0.3. The value 0.1 omits the dz/dw = x factor. The value 3.7 adds the terms instead of multiplying them. The value 1.5 multiplies dL/dy_hat by x but skips the sigmoid derivative.

prompt: A custom model computes the likelihood of 50,000 observations as the product of their individual probabilities, and the result evaluates to exactly 0 in floating point. What should be done?

options.text: Multiply each probability by 10 before taking the product
Maximize the sum of log probabilities, which has the same maximizer
Take the exponential of each probability before multiplying
Maximize the average of the probabilities instead of their product

explanation: Multiplying many numbers below 1 underflows to zero. Because the logarithm is strictly increasing, maximizing the log-likelihood, a sum of log probabilities, gives the same parameters and is numerically stable. Scaling every factor by 10 multiplies the product by 10^50,000, which overflows instead. Exponentiating the probabilities changes the objective without solving the scale problem. Averaging probabilities is a different objective with a different maximizer.

prompt: In three-dimensional space, v1 = (1, 0, 1), v2 = (0, 1, 1) and v3 = (1, 1, 2). Which statement is correct?

options.text: They form a basis because there are three of them in three dimensions
They span all of three-dimensional space but are not a basis because they are not orthogonal
They span only a plane, so they are not a basis for three-dimensional space
They span only a line, because every vector has a 1 in some position

explanation: v3 = v1 + v2, so the set is linearly dependent: the rank is 2 and the span is the plane through v1 and v2. A basis must be linearly independent and span the space, so three vectors are a basis of three-dimensional space only if none is a combination of the others. Orthogonality is not required for a basis. The span is not a line, because v1 and v2 are not multiples of each other.

prompt: For a stationary demand series, the autocorrelation function (ACF) decays gradually, while the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) has significant spikes at lags 1 and 2 and none afterward. Which model is suggested?

options.text: MA(2)
ARIMA(0,1,0)
MA(1)
AR(2)

explanation: An autoregressive process of order p shows a PACF that cuts off after lag p and an ACF that tails off, so a PACF cutoff at lag 2 points to AR(2). A moving-average process shows the reverse pattern: an ACF that cuts off after lag q and a PACF that tails off, so MA(1) and MA(2) do not fit. ARIMA(0,1,0) is a random walk, used when the series is non-stationary, but this series is stationary.

prompt: A one-time supply disruption pushes weekly demand above normal for exactly the two following weeks, after which its effect disappears completely. The analyst wants a model in which a shock affects only a fixed, short number of future periods. Which model structure matches this behaviour?

options.text: An autoregressive model of order 2, in which the current value depends on the last two values
A random walk, in which each shock permanently shifts the level of the series
A moving average model of order 2, in which the current value depends on the last two error terms
An integrated model with second differencing to remove a quadratic trend

explanation: In an MA(q) model the current value is a combination of the current and the previous q shocks, so a shock influences exactly q future periods and then vanishes. In an AR model a shock feeds back through lagged values and decays gradually over many periods rather than stopping. A random walk makes every shock permanent. Second differencing removes a quadratic trend; it does not describe how long a shock lasts.

prompt: A weekly sales series has a clear upward trend. An augmented Dickey-Fuller test on the raw series gives p = 0.62. After first differencing, the test gives p = 0.01. How should the ARIMA model be specified?

options.text: Use d = 0, because a high p value on the raw series shows it is already stationary
Use d = 1, fitting the AR and MA terms to the once-differenced series
Use d = 2, because a trend always requires two differences
Fit an AR model to the raw series and ignore the trend

explanation: The augmented Dickey-Fuller null hypothesis is a unit root (non-stationarity). Failing to reject it on the raw series and rejecting it after one difference means one difference achieves stationarity, so d = 1. A high p value means the test did not show stationarity, so d = 0 is wrong. Differencing twice when once suffices over-differences and adds artificial negative autocorrelation. Fitting AR terms to a trending series violates the stationarity those models assume.

prompt: A study records test scores for the same 800 students every semester for four years, giving 6,400 rows. An analyst fits ordinary least squares treating all rows as independent observations. What is the main problem?

options.text: There is no problem, because 6,400 rows legitimately give eight times the statistical power of 800 rows
Scores from the same student are correlated, so standard errors are understated; use a mixed-effects model
Treat the data as cross-sectional by keeping only each student's final-semester score
Model the data with a single ARIMA model on the average score across students per semester

explanation: In a longitudinal study, measurements on the same subject are not independent, so treating them as independent overstates the effective sample size and understates standard errors. Mixed-effects models or generalized estimating equations (GEE) account for the within-student correlation and allow within-student change to be modelled. The rows do not give 8 times the information. Keeping only the final score throws away the change over time. Averaging across students into one series discards student-level variation.

prompt: In a subscription study, 40 percent of customers are still active when observation ends. An analyst estimates average time to cancellation using only the customers who cancelled. What is wrong, and what should be done?

options.text: The estimate is biased low; treat active customers as right-censored and use a method such as Kaplan-Meier
Nothing is wrong, because active customers have no cancellation time to include
Set each active customer's cancellation time to the study end date and then average across all customers
Fit a linear regression of observed duration on customer attributes and use the intercept

explanation: Dropping customers who have not yet cancelled removes the longest-lived customers, biasing the estimate downward. Survival analysis treats them as right-censored: they are known to have survived at least until the study end. The non-parametric Kaplan-Meier estimator uses that partial information. Using the study end date as the cancellation time still understates their true durations. Ordinary regression on observed durations has the same censoring bias.

prompt: A manufacturer must forecast component failure rates beyond its 24-month follow-up period, and engineering knowledge says the hazard of failure rises with age because of wear. Which survival approach fits best?

options.text: A Kaplan-Meier estimator, which can be read off beyond the last observed time
A parametric exponential model, which assumes the hazard increases with age
A parametric Weibull model with a shape parameter greater than 1
A life table that stops at the last observed 24-month interval

explanation: A parametric survival model assumes a distributional form, which allows extrapolation beyond the observed period, and a Weibull model with shape greater than 1 has a hazard that increases with time, matching wear-out. The non-parametric Kaplan-Meier curve is defined only up to the last observed time and cannot extrapolate. The exponential model assumes a constant hazard, not an increasing one. A life table stops at the observed intervals.

prompt: A causal diagram has two arrows: Talent -> Hired and Connections -> Hired. An analyst looks only at employees who were hired and finds a negative correlation between talent and connections. What explains this?

options.text: Hired is a confounder of talent and connections and must be controlled for
Hired is a mediator through which talent causes a person's connections
The data show that talent directly reduces the number of connections a person has
Hired is a collider, so selecting only hired employees induces a spurious association

explanation: In the directed acyclic graph both arrows point into Hired, which makes it a collider. Conditioning on a collider, here by selecting only hired employees, opens a path between its causes and induces an association that does not exist in the full population; among hires, low talent tends to be offset by strong connections. A confounder would have arrows pointing out to both variables. A mediator would lie on a path from one to the other. The DAG contains no arrow from talent to connections.

prompt: A causal diagram has these arrows: Age -> Exercise, Age -> Blood pressure, Exercise -> Weight, and Weight -> Blood pressure. A researcher wants the total causal effect of exercise on blood pressure. Which variables should the regression adjust for?

options.text: Weight only
Both age and weight
Age only
Neither age nor weight

explanation: Age is a confounder: it opens a backdoor path Exercise <- Age -> Blood pressure, so it must be adjusted for. Weight is a mediator on the causal path Exercise -> Weight -> Blood pressure, and adjusting for it would remove part of the effect being estimated, giving only the direct effect. Adjusting for weight alone leaves confounding by age and also blocks the mediated effect. Adjusting for neither leaves the backdoor path through age open.

prompt: A policy takes effect in Region T but not in Region C. Average monthly sales in Region T were 50 before and 70 after. In Region C they were 40 before and 52 after. What is the difference-in-differences estimate of the policy effect, and what key assumption does it rely on?

options.text: 8; without the policy, both regions would have followed parallel trends
20; Region C's change can be ignored because it did not receive the policy
12; the control region's change is the policy effect
8; the two regions had identical sales levels before the policy

explanation: Difference-in-differences subtracts the control region's change from the treated region's change: (70 - 50) - (52 - 40) = 20 - 12 = 8. It assumes that, absent treatment, the treated region would have changed by the same amount as the control (parallel trends). The value 20 ignores the background change that also occurred in the untreated region. The value 12 is the control region's change itself. The method does not require equal starting levels, only parallel trends.

prompt: During an A/B test of a new pricing page, the team checks the dashboard every day and plans to stop as soon as the p value drops below 0.05. On day 6, the p value is 0.04 and they stop. What is the main concern?

options.text: Six days is too short for any online experiment, so the result must be reported as a negative finding
A p value of 0.04 proves the new page is better with 96 percent probability
Daily checks reduce statistical power, so a real effect was probably missed
Repeated peeking with optional stopping inflates the false positive rate well above 5 percent

explanation: Each look is another chance for random noise to cross the threshold, so stopping at the first significant look makes the real Type I error rate much higher than the nominal 5 percent. The fix is a pre-registered sample size or a sequential testing method designed for interim looks. Test duration alone does not make the result negative. A p value is not the probability that the variant is better. The problem with peeking is too many false positives, not lost power.

prompt: Observational data show that users who turned on a new reminders feature retain 30 percent better than users who did not. The product team wants to claim that the feature causes higher retention. What is the most reliable way to establish this?

options.text: Collect another year of observational data to confirm the correlation
Compare retention for all users before and after the feature was released
A randomized controlled trial that randomly enables the feature for some users
Compute the correlation on a larger sample to reduce the p value

explanation: Users who opt in to the feature are likely more engaged to begin with, so the comparison is confounded by self-selection. Random assignment makes the groups comparable on both measured and unmeasured characteristics, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to the feature. More observational data or a larger sample shrinks random error but not confounding bias. A before-and-after comparison is confounded by anything else that changed over the same period.

prompt: A Q-Q plot compares a regression model's residuals against a normal distribution. The points in the middle lie on the reference line, the lower-left points stay close to it, and the upper-right points rise well above it. What does this indicate?

options.text: The residuals have a heavier right tail than a normal distribution
The residuals are normally distributed
The residuals have lighter tails than a normal distribution in both directions
The residual variance increases with the fitted values

explanation: On a quantile-quantile plot, sample quantiles above the line in the upper right mean the largest residuals are larger than a normal distribution predicts, so the right tail is heavy (right skew). Normal residuals would follow the line throughout. Light tails would bend the upper-right points below the line and the lower-left points above it. A Q-Q plot shows the shape of the marginal distribution, not how variance changes with fitted values; a residual versus fitted plot shows that.

prompt: Box plots of session duration for three app versions look nearly identical, but the analyst suspects one version has two distinct groups of users, one with very short and one with very long sessions. Which chart would reveal this best?

options.text: A bar plot of mean session duration by app version
A line plot of median session duration by app version
A violin plot of session duration by app version
A Sankey diagram of users flowing between app versions

explanation: A violin plot shows the estimated density at every value, so a bimodal distribution appears as two bulges, which a box plot's five-number summary can hide. A bar plot of means collapses each distribution to one number. A line plot implies an ordered or continuous axis and still shows only one statistic. A Sankey diagram shows flows between states, not the distribution of a continuous variable.

prompt: A product team wants to show how 10,000 trial users moved from the trial into Basic, Premium or churned, and then how those users moved between tiers three months later, with flow widths proportional to user counts. Which visualization fits best?

options.text: A scatter plot matrix
A Sankey diagram
A correlation heat map
A Q-Q plot

explanation: A Sankey diagram draws flows between stages with widths proportional to quantity, which is exactly what tier-to-tier movement requires. A scatter plot matrix shows pairwise relationships among numeric variables. A correlation heat map shows correlation coefficients between variables, not movement of entities. A Q-Q plot compares a distribution with a reference distribution.

prompt: Before modelling, an analyst wants to see the shape of every pairwise relationship among six continuous variables, including any curvature, clusters or outliers. Which visualization serves this best?

options.text: A correlation heat map of the six variables
A scatter plot matrix
Six separate histograms
A stacked bar plot of the six variables

explanation: A scatter plot matrix shows a scatter plot for every pair of variables, so curvature, clusters and outliers are visible directly. A correlation heat map reduces each pair to one coefficient, which can hide non-linear patterns and outliers. Histograms are univariate and show no relationships. A stacked bar plot compares totals and parts of categories, not relationships between continuous variables.

prompt: A data set has 45 numeric features. The analyst wants a single compact view to spot groups of features that are strongly correlated with each other before checking multicollinearity. Which visualization is most appropriate?

options.text: A scatter plot matrix showing all 45 features pairwise
A box and whisker plot for each of the 45 features
A correlation heat map with features ordered by clustering
A line plot of each feature against its row number

explanation: A correlation heat map encodes each pairwise coefficient as a colour, and ordering features by clustering places correlated groups together as visible blocks. A 45-variable scatter plot matrix has 990 distinct panels, too many to read. Box plots are univariate and show nothing about correlation. Plotting features against row number shows ordering artefacts, not relationships between features.

prompt: An analyst wants to compare the distributions of delivery time for three carriers on one chart. Overlaid histograms are cluttered because their bars hide each other. Which alternative is most effective?

options.text: A pie chart of total deliveries per carrier
Overlaid density plots, one curve per carrier
A single histogram of all deliveries combined
A bar plot of the number of deliveries per carrier

explanation: Density plots draw each distribution as a smooth curve, so several can be overlaid and compared for centre, spread and shape without bars hiding each other. A pie chart shows shares of a total, not distributions. Combining all deliveries into one histogram removes the carrier comparison. A bar plot of counts shows volume, not the distribution of delivery times.

prompt: For a variable with first quartile 20 and third quartile 40, a box and whisker plot marks points beyond 1.5 times the interquartile range from the box as outliers. Which two of these values would be plotted as outliers?
explanation: The interquartile range is 40 - 20 = 20, so the fences are 20 - 1.5 x 20 = -10 and 40 + 1.5 x 20 = 70. Only 75 (above 70) and -12 (below -10) fall outside the fences. The value 68 is above the box but inside the upper fence. The values 5 and 45 are outside the box but within the whiskers' reach, so they are not marked as outliers.

prompt: For an executive slide, an analyst needs to compare the number of support tickets across 12 product categories that have no natural order. Which chart is most appropriate?

options.text: A line plot connecting the 12 category counts
A histogram of ticket counts
A pie chart with 12 slices
A bar plot with bars sorted by ticket count

explanation: Bar plots compare a quantity across discrete categories, and sorting the bars makes ranking easy to read. A line plot implies a continuous or ordered axis, such as time, so connecting unordered categories suggests a trend that does not exist. A histogram shows the distribution of a continuous variable, not counts per category. A 12-slice pie chart forces comparison of angles, which people judge less accurately than bar lengths.

prompt: A scatter plot of 2 million transactions, with amount against customer age, appears as a solid block of colour, hiding where points are concentrated. Which change best reveals the structure?

options.text: Increase the marker size so each point is easier to see
Switch to a line plot sorted by customer age
Replace the chart with a Sankey diagram of age groups
Use hexagonal binning or transparency to show point density

explanation: With millions of points, overplotting hides density; hexagonal binning (or a 2-D density plot) counts points per cell, and transparency lets dense areas build up darker colour. Larger markers make the overplotting worse. A line plot connects points in order and implies a sequence, which is meaningless for independent transactions. A Sankey diagram shows flows between stages, not the relationship between two continuous variables.

prompt: Identify the feature types: ZIP code; number of children in the household; customer satisfaction rated from very dissatisfied to very satisfied; has_loyalty_card (yes or no).

options.text: Nominal; discrete; ordinal; binary
Continuous; discrete; nominal; binary
Nominal; continuous; ordinal; nominal
Ordinal; discrete; continuous; binary

explanation: ZIP codes are labels with no meaningful order or arithmetic, so they are nominal despite being numeric. Number of children is a count, so it is discrete. A satisfaction scale has ordered categories with unequal or unknown spacing, so it is ordinal. A yes or no flag is binary. Treating ZIP codes as continuous or ordinal implies arithmetic or ordering that does not exist. Counts of children cannot take fractional values, so they are not continuous.

prompt: A field called product_code stores integers from 1001 to 4000, one per product. An EDA report lists its mean as 2,512 and its standard deviation as 860. What is the problem?

options.text: The mean is acceptable, but a median should be reported instead because of skew
The standard deviation is too large, which shows the codes contain data entry errors
It is a nominal identifier, so frequency counts are appropriate and a mean is meaningless
product_code is a continuous measure, so a histogram should be added to the report

explanation: An identifier stored as an integer is still a label: the arithmetic difference between codes means nothing, so its mean and standard deviation are meaningless. Category frequencies, the number of distinct values and the most common codes are the appropriate summaries. Switching to a median still treats the codes as quantities. The spread of codes reflects how they were assigned, not errors. It is not continuous, so a histogram of code values would also mislead.

prompt: An analyst receives a new claim_amount column and wants to understand it before using it in any model. Which first step is most appropriate?

options.text: Fit a multiple regression model with claim_amount as the target variable
Build a correlation heat map of claim_amount against every other variable
Run a chi-squared test of independence between claim_amount and region
Univariate analysis: summary statistics, missing counts, range and a histogram

explanation: Univariate analysis examines one variable on its own (its distribution, range, centre, spread, missing values and anomalies such as negative amounts or placeholder codes), which must come before relating it to anything else. Fitting a regression or a correlation heat map are multivariate steps that can be distorted by problems a univariate check would have found. A chi-squared test applies to two categorical variables, and claim_amount is continuous.

prompt: Overall, treatment A succeeds in 78 percent of cases and treatment B in 83 percent. Within mild cases and within severe cases separately, A has the higher success rate. Treatment A was given mostly to severe cases. What is happening?

options.text: Sampling error: with enough data the within-group results would come to match the overall result
Simpson's paradox: severity confounds the comparison, so the stratified result should be trusted
Multicollinearity between treatment and severity makes both comparisons unreliable
The overall result is correct, because stratifying the data always introduces bias

explanation: When a third variable is related to both the treatment and the outcome, an aggregate comparison can reverse within every subgroup (Simpson's paradox). Because A was given mostly to severe cases, which succeed less often, its overall rate is pulled down; multivariate analysis that conditions on severity gives the fair comparison. More data would not remove a structural confounder. Multicollinearity is about correlated predictors inflating variance in regression. Stratifying on a confounder removes bias rather than adding it.

prompt: An analyst is building customer profiles from a CRM table and from application event logs. Which two of these are behavioural features rather than static attributes?

options.text: Median days between purchases
Plan tier at sign-up
Average number of logins per week
Date of birth
Customer region

explanation: Behavioural features summarise what an entity does over time, such as login frequency or purchase intervals derived from event logs. Region, date of birth and plan tier at sign-up are attributes that describe the customer and do not come from observed activity. Separating attributes from behaviours helps decide which data sources to join and how often each feature needs refreshing.

prompt: A histogram of online order values with the default bin width shows a single smooth peak. The analyst suspects many orders cluster just above the $50 free-shipping threshold. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Replace the histogram with a box plot, which shows every peak in the data
Log-transform the order values so the peak disappears
Switch to a pie chart of orders above and below $50
Redraw the histogram with narrower bins aligned to the $50 threshold

explanation: A histogram's appearance depends on bin width and bin edges; wide bins can merge a spike just above $50 into its neighbours, so narrower bins with an edge at $50 show whether the cluster exists. A box plot summarises with quartiles and cannot show a local spike. Log-transforming changes the scale but does not fix the binning problem. A pie chart of two groups removes the distribution entirely.

prompt: One-hot encoding 60,000 product IDs for 2 million rows produces a matrix in which more than 99.99 percent of the entries are zero. Converting it to a dense 64-bit array would need about 960 GB. What should the team do?

options.text: Store it in a sparse format such as compressed sparse row and use sparse-aware algorithms
Convert the dense array to 32-bit floats so that it uses half the memory
Label-encode the product IDs into one integer column and then standardize that column
Drop every one-hot column whose values are mostly zero to reduce the width

explanation: A sparse matrix format stores only the non-zero entries and their positions, so memory scales with the number of non-zeros (about 2 million here) rather than rows times columns. Halving precision still needs about 480 GB. Label encoding avoids the size problem but imposes a false numeric order on IDs. Every one-hot column is mostly zeros, so dropping them would discard all the product information.

prompt: In a user-item rating matrix, the average user has rated 8 of 50,000 items. A user-based recommender computes cosine similarity between users' rating vectors, and most pairs share zero or one rated item. What is the main issue?

options.text: The vectors are too dense, so every user looks almost equally similar to every other user
Cosine similarity cannot be computed for vectors that contain zeros
The ratings are non-stationary, so similarities drift over time
The vectors are so sparse that similarities rest on almost no overlap and are unreliable

explanation: With sparse vectors, most pairs of users share few or no rated items, so a similarity based on one shared rating is noise; latent-factor methods such as matrix factorization, or item-based similarity with shrinkage, are common remedies. The vectors are sparse, not dense. Cosine similarity handles zeros fine; the issue is how little overlap the non-zero entries have. Drift over time is a separate concern that does not explain missing overlap.

prompt: A linear model predicts fuel consumption from vehicle speed. A plot of residuals against speed shows a clear U shape: positive at low and high speeds and negative at moderate speeds. What does this indicate, and what is a reasonable remedy?

options.text: A non-linear relationship; add a squared speed term or use splines
Heteroskedasticity; refit using weighted least squares
Multicollinearity; remove speed from the regression model and refit it
Autocorrelation; add a lagged residual term to the model

explanation: A systematic curved pattern in residuals against a predictor means the straight-line form is wrong for that predictor, so a polynomial term, splines or a non-linear model is needed. Heteroskedasticity shows as changing spread, not a curved mean. Multicollinearity involves two or more correlated predictors, and there is only one here. Autocorrelation concerns the order of observations, not a pattern against speed.

prompt: An analyst regresses one company's monthly revenue on an unrelated country's monthly population over ten years. Both series trend upward. The regression gives R2 = 0.92, but the residuals are strongly autocorrelated. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: Revenue is genuinely driven by that country's population
A sparse data problem caused by having only 120 observations
A spurious regression caused by non-stationary trending series
Granularity misalignment between monthly and annual data

explanation: Two series that both trend over time will correlate strongly even when unrelated; non-stationarity breaks the usual inference, and strongly autocorrelated residuals are a warning sign. Differencing the series or testing for cointegration addresses it. A high R2 alone is not evidence of causation. 120 observations with no missing cells are not sparse. Both series are monthly, so there is no granularity misalignment.

prompt: Advertising spend affects sales two to three weeks later. An analyst building a weekly sales model wants to capture this effect without leaking future information. Which features should be created?

options.text: Ad spend two and three weeks ahead of the sales week
A rolling average of ad spend centred on the sales week
Ad spend lagged by two and three weeks
Only the current week's ad spend, since lags add multicollinearity

explanation: Lagged observations, the spend from t - 2 and t - 3, align the cause with its delayed effect, and they are known at prediction time. Spend from future weeks is not available when forecasting and leaks information from after the target period. A centred rolling average also includes future weeks. Using only the current week misses the delayed effect entirely.

prompt: A model is trained on first differences of daily inventory (today's level minus yesterday's). Today's inventory is 120 units, and the model forecasts a difference of +5 for tomorrow. What is the forecast inventory level for tomorrow?

options.text: 5 units
115 units
600 units
125 units

explanation: A model on differenced observations predicts the change, so the level forecast is the last observed level plus the predicted change: 120 + 5 = 125. Reporting 5 confuses the change with the level. Subtracting gives 115, reversing the definition of the difference. Multiplying the level by the change has no basis in differencing.

prompt: A retailer reports that December sales rose 40 percent over November and credits a new marketing campaign. Every previous year, December sales were 35 to 45 percent above November. What is the best response?

options.text: Accept the claim, because a 40 percent increase is too large to be due to chance
Compare December with the average of January to November sales this year
Note the seasonality and compare with prior Decembers or a seasonally adjusted series
Remove December from the data as an outlier before evaluating the campaign

explanation: Sales have a recurring annual pattern, so a December jump is expected regardless of the campaign; year-over-year comparison or seasonal adjustment isolates the campaign effect. A large change is not evidence of a cause when it matches the usual seasonal pattern. Comparing with the January to November average still mixes in seasonality. December is a regular seasonal peak, not an outlier.

prompt: A house price regression includes square footage and number of rooms. The overall F test is highly significant, but neither coefficient is individually significant, their standard errors are large, and the room coefficient is negative. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Heteroskedasticity in the house price residuals
Multicollinearity between square footage and number of rooms
Non-stationarity of house prices over the sample period
Insufficient features in the house price model

explanation: When predictors are strongly correlated, the model cannot separate their individual effects, so coefficients have large standard errors, unexpected signs and low individual significance while the joint F test remains strong. Heteroskedasticity distorts standard errors but does not typically flip signs while the joint fit stays strong. Non-stationarity concerns time series. The joint significance shows the features carry signal, so missing features is not the issue.

prompt: A daily sales table is joined to a monthly marketing budget table by copying each month's budget onto every day of that month. A regression of daily sales on budget then reports a very small p value for budget. What is the problem?

options.text: Granularity misalignment: copies of one monthly value act as independent rows
Seasonality: daily sales vary systematically by the day of the week
Sparse data: most days in the joined table have no marketing budget value recorded
Lagged observations: the budget should be shifted forward by one day

explanation: The budget varies only monthly, so repeating it daily inflates the apparent sample size about thirtyfold and makes the standard error far too small. Aggregating sales to the monthly grain, or using a model that respects the grouping, aligns the data. Day-of-week seasonality may exist but does not explain the inflated significance. Every day has a budget value, so the data are not sparse. A one-day lag does not fix the mismatch in grain.

prompt: A learning curve for a gradient-boosted model shows training error and validation error both high and close together. Doubling the training data leaves both almost unchanged. What is the most likely problem, and what should be done?

options.text: Overfitting; add stronger regularization to the model
Too little data; collect several times more training rows
Insufficient features; add more informative predictors
Data leakage; remove the single most predictive feature

explanation: High, converged training and validation errors that do not improve with more data mean the inputs do not contain enough signal about the target, so new or better features are needed. Overfitting shows low training error with much higher validation error. More rows did not help, ruling out insufficient data. Leakage produces unrealistically low validation error, not uniformly high error.

prompt: In a customer table, one record shows age 12 and annual income $250,000. Each value lies within the normal range of its own column, so univariate outlier checks did not flag it. Which method would detect such records?

options.text: A z-score threshold applied to each column separately
Interquartile range fences computed for each column separately, then combined
Mahalanobis distance or an isolation forest on the joint distribution
Trimming the top and bottom 1 percent of values in each column

explanation: A multivariate outlier is an unusual combination of values, so detecting it requires methods that consider variables jointly; Mahalanobis distance accounts for the correlation between features, and an isolation forest isolates unusual combinations. Z-scores, IQR fences and per-column trimming all examine one variable at a time, so a record whose individual values are each ordinary passes all of them.

prompt: A linear regression uses a region feature with four values (North, South, East, West) that has been coded as the integers 1 to 4. Which encoding is more appropriate, and why?

options.text: One-hot encoding with one level dropped, because integer codes impose a false order
Keep the label encoding, because linear models handle any integer codes correctly
Standardize the integer codes so that they have mean 0 and standard deviation 1
One-hot encoding of all four levels plus an intercept, so no level is lost

explanation: Region is nominal, so label encoding tells a linear model that West is four times North and that the regions are equally spaced. One-hot encoding creates one indicator per level, and dropping one level as the reference avoids perfect collinearity with the intercept (the dummy variable trap). Standardizing the integer codes keeps the false order. Keeping all four indicators alongside an intercept makes the design matrix rank-deficient.

prompt: A pricing analyst finds that the effect of a discount on unit sales is much larger in urban stores than in rural stores. The current linear model has discount and an urban indicator as separate terms. What should be added?

options.text: A squared discount term to capture curvature in its effect
An interaction term equal to discount multiplied by the urban indicator
A log transformation of the unit sales target only
A min-max scaled copy of the discount feature alongside the original

explanation: A cross-term (interaction) lets the slope of discount differ between urban and rural stores, which is what the finding describes. A squared term models curvature in discount's effect, not dependence on location. Log-transforming the target changes the scale of effects but still gives one discount slope for both store types. Rescaling discount changes its units, not its relationship to location.

prompt: A company's revenue has grown by roughly 8 percent per year for 15 years, so a plot of revenue against year curves upward. The analyst wants a linear model whose slope is easy to interpret. Which transformation is most appropriate?

options.text: Model revenue as a linear function of the natural log of year
Model revenue as a linear function of year squared
Standardize revenue and keep a linear model in year
Model the natural log of revenue as a linear function of year

explanation: Constant percentage growth is exponential, so taking the logarithm of revenue linearizes it: ln(revenue) = a + b x year, with b approximately equal to the annual growth rate. Logging the year bends the curve the wrong way for exponential growth. A squared year term approximates curvature but does not represent constant percentage growth and has no growth-rate interpretation. Standardizing is a linear rescaling and leaves the curve unchanged.

prompt: A model was trained to predict the natural log of house price. The business needs predictions in dollars. What should be done with the model's outputs?

options.text: Exponentiate them, noting this estimates median rather than mean price
Take their logarithm again so that the units return to dollars
Multiply them by the average house price in the training data
Report them directly, because a log is only a rescaling of dollars

explanation: The exponential function is the inverse of the natural log, so exponentiating returns predictions to dollars. Because the mean of a log is not the log of the mean, exp of the predicted mean log estimates the median; a smearing correction is needed if the mean is wanted. Taking another log moves further from dollars. Multiplying by an average price has no mathematical basis. Log units are not a linear rescaling of dollars, so they cannot be reported directly.

prompt: An analyst wants a Box-Cox transformation to reduce skew in an account-balance feature, but the feature contains zeros and negative values. What is the best option?

options.text: Apply Box-Cox with lambda set to 0, which is designed to handle zeros
Apply a natural log transformation directly to the raw balances
Apply a square root transformation directly to the raw balances
Use a Yeo-Johnson transformation, which allows zero and negative values

explanation: Box-Cox is defined only for strictly positive values. Yeo-Johnson is a related power-transformation family that works for zero and negative values. Lambda = 0 in Box-Cox is the natural log, which is undefined at zero and for negatives. A direct log fails for the same reason, and a square root is undefined for negative values.

prompt: Feature A has minimum 10 and maximum 60. Feature B has mean 50 and standard deviation 8. A record has A = 30 and B = 70. What are the min-max normalized value of A and the standardized (z-score) value of B?

options.text: A = 0.4 and B = 20

explanation: Min-max normalization gives (30 - 10)/(60 - 10) = 20/50 = 0.4. Standardization gives (70 - 50)/8 = 2.5. The value 0.5 divides 30 by the maximum without subtracting the minimum. The value 20 is the raw deviation from the mean, without dividing by the standard deviation. The value 0.6 is the distance from the maximum, (60 - 30)/50, rather than from the minimum.

prompt: A ridge regression is fitted on unscaled features. A colleague changes a distance feature from metres to kilometres, and the model's predictions and the shrinkage of that feature change noticeably. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: Ridge regression is unstable for any feature measured in kilometres; convert all features to metres
The L2 penalty depends on coefficient size, which depends on units; standardize features before fitting
The change introduced multicollinearity; remove the distance feature
Ridge regression ignores units, so the change must come from a bug in the pipeline

explanation: Rescaling a feature by 1/1,000 multiplies its coefficient by 1,000, so the same L2 penalty shrinks it very differently. Scaling all features to comparable ranges, usually by standardization, makes the penalty treat them evenly and makes results independent of units. No unit is inherently unstable; the issue is inconsistent scaling. A unit change does not create correlation with other features. Unpenalized OLS is unit-invariant in its predictions, but ridge is not.

prompt: A regulator requires a credit scorecard in which each applicant receives a fixed number of points for falling within an age band, such as 18 to 25 or 26 to 35. How should age be prepared?

options.text: Bin age into the defined ranges and assign each band its own points
Keep age as a continuous feature with a single coefficient for all ages
One-hot encode every distinct age in years
Apply a Box-Cox transformation to age

explanation: Binning converts a continuous variable into intervals, which matches a scorecard that awards points per band and can capture non-linear, step-like effects, at the cost of some information lost within each band. A single continuous coefficient gives points proportional to age rather than per band. One-hot encoding every year creates many sparse indicators and does not produce the required bands. A Box-Cox transformation keeps age continuous.

prompt: A lender has columns for monthly debt payments and monthly gross income. A linear model using both as separate features performs worse than expected, and underwriters say affordability is what matters. Which engineered feature best captures this?

options.text: The sum of monthly debt payments and monthly gross income per applicant
Monthly gross income binned into five equal-width ranges
The debt-to-income ratio: monthly debt payments divided by gross income
One-hot encoded monthly debt payment amounts

explanation: A ratio feature expresses one quantity relative to another, so the same debt means different risk at different incomes, which a linear model with separate additive terms cannot represent directly. Adding debt and income produces a number with no risk interpretation. Binning income discards information and ignores debt. One-hot encoding continuous payment amounts creates many sparse columns with no notion of affordability.

prompt: A transactions table has one row per purchase with the columns customer_id, category and amount. A churn model needs one row per customer with total spend in each of eight categories as separate columns. Which operation produces this?

options.text: Pivoting from long to wide, summing amount by customer and category
A union of the transactions table with itself
One-hot encoding category while keeping one row per individual purchase
Binning amount into eight equal-width intervals

explanation: Pivoting turns the values of one column (category) into separate columns and aggregates a measure (sum of amount) for each combination, giving one row per customer. A union stacks rows and keeps the long shape. One-hot encoding creates indicator columns but still has one row per purchase. Binning amount groups spending levels and has nothing to do with categories.

prompt: A delivery-time model has the customer's street address as text. The team suspects distance from the nearest warehouse drives delivery time. What is the best first step to use this information?

options.text: One-hot encode the full street address so that each distinct location gets its own column
Label-encode the street names in alphabetical order as integer codes
Geocode each address to coordinates and compute distance to the nearest warehouse
Compute the character length of each address as a numeric feature

explanation: Geocoding converts an address into geographic coordinates, from which a distance feature can be calculated. One-hot encoding full addresses produces a near-unique indicator per row with no notion of proximity. Alphabetical label codes carry no geographic meaning. Address length is unrelated to location.

prompt: A team has 1,200 labelled defect images and plans to enlarge the training data with flipped, rotated and cropped copies, plus synthetic images from a generative model fitted to the training set. Which two practices are appropriate?

options.text: Fit the generative model on all images, including the test set, for better fidelity
Apply augmentation and synthetic generation to the training split only
Measure final performance on a held-out set of real, unaugmented images
Augment the validation and test sets as well, to make them larger
Include transformations that change the true label, because they add variety

explanation: Augmented and synthetic data should enrich training only, and evaluation must use real held-out images so that the performance estimate reflects real-world inputs. Augmenting evaluation sets inflates their size with near-duplicates and makes the estimate unrepresentative. Fitting the generator on test images leaks test information into training. Transformations that change the correct label, such as flipping an asymmetric defect type, add label noise rather than useful variety.
