explanation: Batch normalization standardizes a layer's inputs using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch during training, then applies a learned scale and shift; at inference it uses running averages collected during training, so predictions work for any batch size, including one. It often stabilizes training and allows higher learning rates. It operates inside the network, not as a one-off preprocessing step. It does not replace the optimizer.

prompt: A team trains for 200 epochs and keeps the final weights. Validation loss reached its minimum at epoch 45 and rose afterward. Which technique should they use?

options.text: Training for 400 epochs so the validation loss has time to decline again later
Batch normalization added after the output layer to stop the rise in validation loss
A larger batch size, so that the validation loss stops rising after epoch 45
Early stopping with patience, restoring the weights from the best validation epoch

explanation: Early stopping monitors validation loss, stops once it has not improved for a set number of epochs (patience), and restores the best weights, preventing the overfitting seen after epoch 45. Training longer extends the overfitting. Batch normalization after the output layer does not prevent overfitting. Batch size changes the noise in gradient estimates but does not reliably stop overfitting.

prompt: Training loss falls quickly at first and then plateaus with small oscillations, although the model has not converged. Which change is most likely to help?

options.text: A fixed, larger learning rate for the remaining epochs to escape the plateau region
Removing the bias terms from every layer so there are fewer parameters to update
Shuffling the validation data each epoch so the reported validation loss varies more
A learning rate scheduler that lowers the rate on plateau or on a decay schedule

explanation: Oscillation around a plateau often means steps are too large to settle into a lower region of the loss surface; a scheduler that lowers the learning rate when progress stalls, or decays it over time (for example step or cosine schedules), lets the optimizer make finer progress. A larger fixed rate tends to increase oscillation. Removing biases reduces capacity without addressing step size. Shuffling validation data does not affect training.

prompt: Which statement best describes the role of back propagation in training a neural network?

options.text: It applies the chain rule backward from the loss to compute the gradient for every weight
It updates every weight by a fixed amount in the direction that the last layer requires
It passes inputs backward through the network to reconstruct the original training data
It chooses the network architecture by removing layers whose weights change the least

explanation: Back propagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter by applying the chain rule layer by layer from the output backward, reusing intermediate results; an optimizer such as SGD or Adam then uses those gradients to update the weights. It does not apply fixed-size updates. Reconstructing inputs describes an autoencoder's objective, not back propagation. Choosing architectures is a separate design or search process.

prompt: A retailer wants to classify product photos into 50 new categories for which it has no labelled images at all, only a short text description of each category. Which approach fits this situation?

options.text: One-shot learning, training on a single labelled image for each new category
Few-shot learning, fine-tuning on a handful of labelled images per category
Zero-shot learning, matching images to category descriptions in a shared space
Supervised learning from scratch on the existing catalogue's labelled categories

explanation: Zero-shot learning recognises classes with no labelled examples by relating inputs to semantic descriptions, for example with a model that embeds images and text in a shared space and picks the closest description. One-shot learning needs one labelled example per class, and few-shot learning needs a handful; the retailer has none. Training from scratch on existing categories cannot predict categories it has never seen.

prompt: A small analytics team with limited deep-learning expertise needs a reasonable image classifier quickly and wants the system to search architectures and hyperparameters automatically. Which tool category fits best?

options.text: Writing a custom training loop in PyTorch with a hand-designed architecture
A custom Keras network built and tuned by hand
An AutoML tool that automates model and hyperparameter search
Implementing back propagation from scratch in NumPy to control every step

explanation: AutoML tools automate model selection, architecture search and hyperparameter tuning, which suits a team that needs results quickly without deep-learning specialists. PyTorch and TensorFlow/Keras are flexible frameworks, but hand-designing and tuning a network requires the expertise the team lacks. Implementing back propagation from scratch is slow, error-prone and unnecessary.

prompt: Which statement about the Adam optimizer is correct?

options.text: It uses a single global learning rate and no gradient history, like plain stochastic gradient descent
It computes exact second derivatives of the loss, like Newton's method, at every training step
It processes the full data set in every step, so it cannot be used with mini-batches of data
It combines momentum with RMSprop-style per-parameter learning rates scaled by recent squared gradients

explanation: Adam keeps an exponentially decaying average of past gradients (momentum, which smooths and accelerates updates) and of past squared gradients (as in RMSprop, which scales each parameter's step), with bias correction for early steps. Plain SGD has no adaptive scaling or momentum. Adam uses first-order gradients only, not second derivatives. Adam is normally used with mini-batches.

prompt: A team cannot fit its full training set into GPU memory for each update, and plain stochastic gradient descent with one example per step is noisy and slow on the hardware. Which approach balances these concerns?

options.text: Mini-batch gradient descent with batches of, for example, 64 to 512 examples
Full-batch gradient descent that loads the whole training set for every update
Pure stochastic gradient descent with one example per update to minimise memory
Training with no gradient updates, keeping the network's random initial weights

explanation: Mini-batches give gradient estimates that are less noisy than single examples, make good use of GPU parallelism, and fit in memory, which is why they are the standard choice. Full-batch updates do not fit in memory here. One example per step underuses the GPU and has high gradient noise. A network with no updates does not learn.

prompt: Which pairing of deep-learning model type and task is most appropriate?

options.text: A basic RNN for long sequences, because it avoids vanishing gradients better than an LSTM
A CNN for long text sequences, because only CNNs can model word order in a sentence
An LSTM for forecasting from long sensor sequences with long-range dependencies
An autoencoder for multiclass image labelling, because it outputs class probabilities

explanation: Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks use input, forget and output gates and a cell state to carry information across long sequences, mitigating the vanishing gradients that make basic RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies. Basic RNNs are worse than LSTMs at this, not better. CNNs can model local word order, but they are not the only option; RNNs and transformers also do so. An autoencoder learns to reconstruct its input and does not output class probabilities.

prompt: A GAN trained to generate product images produces only a few nearly identical images regardless of the random input. What is this failure called, and which part of the GAN is affected?

options.text: Overfitting; the discriminator memorizes the training images and outputs copies of them
Vanishing gradients; the discriminator stops producing images and outputs random noise
Mode collapse; the generator maps many inputs to a few outputs that fool the discriminator
Data leakage; the generator copies the test set images, which makes them identical

explanation: A generative adversarial network has a generator that creates samples and a discriminator that tries to tell them from real data. Mode collapse occurs when the generator finds a few outputs that reliably fool the discriminator and stops covering the variety of the real data. The discriminator classifies; it does not output images. Vanishing gradients can stall training but do not produce a few repeated images. Leakage is an evaluation flaw, not a generation failure.

prompt: A manufacturer has thousands of images of normal parts but very few images of defective ones. Which deep-learning approach is well suited to flagging defects?

options.text: Train an autoencoder on normal images and flag parts with high reconstruction error
Train a GAN discriminator on defective images only and flag parts it rates as real
Train a softmax classifier with one class, normal, and flag low-confidence predictions
Train an LSTM on the images in random order and flag parts with unusual hidden states

explanation: An autoencoder trained only on normal parts learns to reconstruct them well; defective parts differ from what it learned, so they reconstruct poorly, and a high reconstruction error flags them as anomalies. Training on the few defective images gives too little data and learns the wrong target. A softmax over a single class always outputs probability 1, so it has no confidence signal. An LSTM models sequences, and random image ordering has no sequential structure.

prompt: Why have transformers largely replaced RNNs for long-text tasks, and what cost do they bring?

options.text: They process tokens one at a time, so cost grows linearly
Transformers do not need positional information, because attention captures word order
Transformers use pooling layers to discard most tokens, which keeps their cost constant
Self-attention relates all positions in parallel, at a cost quadratic in length

explanation: Self-attention lets every token attend directly to every other token, capturing long-range dependencies and allowing parallel computation across the sequence, unlike an RNN's step-by-step processing. Comparing every pair of tokens makes standard attention's compute and memory grow with the square of sequence length. Processing one token at a time describes RNNs. Attention alone is order-invariant, so transformers add positional encodings. Transformers do not rely on pooling to discard tokens.

prompt: k-means inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) for k = 1 to 6 is: 1000, 520, 300, 270, 250, 235. Using the elbow method, which k is most reasonable?
explanation: The elbow is where adding clusters stops giving large reductions: from 1 to 2 the drop is 480, from 2 to 3 it is 220, and after that only 30, 20 and 15. The curve bends at k = 3. At k = 2 a large reduction is still available by adding a third cluster. Beyond 3 the gains are small, and k = 6 has the lowest inertia only because inertia always falls as k grows.

prompt: For a customer segmentation, the average silhouette scores are 0.18 for k = 3, 0.52 for k = 4 and 0.31 for k = 5. Some points in the k = 5 solution have negative silhouette values. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: k = 3 is best, because lower silhouette means tighter clusters
k = 5 is best, because negative silhouette values show that the clusters are well separated
Silhouette scores cannot compare different values of k, so the elbow method must be used
k = 4 is best; negative values mark points closer to another cluster than their own

explanation: The silhouette compares each point's mean distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other cluster, ranging from -1 to 1; higher averages mean better-defined clusters, so k = 4 is best. A negative value means a point is, on average, closer to a neighbouring cluster, suggesting misassignment. Lower scores indicate worse, not tighter, clustering. Average silhouette is a standard way to compare different values of k.

prompt: GPS points of vehicle stops form long, curved clusters of varying shape, with scattered isolated points that should not belong to any cluster. k-means produces poor results. Which algorithm is more appropriate?

options.text: k-means with a larger k, which will follow the curved clusters more closely
DBSCAN, which groups dense regions of any shape and labels isolated points as noise
k-means on standardized coordinates, which makes the clusters become spherical
PCA followed by k-means, which removes the noise points before the clustering step

explanation: DBSCAN defines clusters as regions where points have at least min_samples neighbours within distance eps, so it finds arbitrarily shaped clusters and marks points in sparse areas as noise. k-means assumes roughly spherical clusters around centroids and assigns every point to a cluster, so a larger k just chops curves into pieces. Standardizing does not make curved clusters spherical. PCA reduces dimensions but does not identify noise points.

prompt: A DBSCAN model works well in a dense city centre but labels most points in the sparser suburbs as noise. No single eps value works for both areas. Which option addresses this?

options.text: k-means with k chosen from the elbow method, applied to both areas together
DBSCAN with min_samples set to 1, so that every point becomes a core point
DBSCAN with eps set to the maximum distance between any pair of points
HDBSCAN, which builds a density hierarchy and finds clusters of varying density

explanation: DBSCAN uses one global density threshold, so it struggles when cluster densities differ; HDBSCAN extends it hierarchically over many density levels and extracts stable clusters of different densities. k-means does not model density and still assumes spherical clusters. With min_samples 1, every point is a core point, so noise detection is lost. A huge eps merges everything into one cluster.

prompt: A biologist wants to cluster 300 tissue samples without choosing the number of clusters in advance, and wants to see how clusters merge at different similarity levels. Which method and output fit best?

options.text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering, read from a dendrogram cut at a chosen height
k-means clustering, read from the centroids reported for a preset value of k
DBSCAN clustering, read from the core points it identifies at a single eps value
t-SNE embedding, read from the distances between the clusters shown in the plot

explanation: Hierarchical clustering repeatedly merges the closest clusters and records the sequence in a dendrogram, so the number of clusters can be chosen afterwards by cutting at a height, and merge levels show nested structure. With 300 samples, its quadratic memory cost is not a problem. k-means requires k in advance. DBSCAN gives one flat clustering per eps. t-SNE is a visualization method, and distances between its clusters are not reliable.

prompt: An analyst will run PCA on five features in different units, including income in dollars (variance about 10^8) and age in years (variance about 100). After standardizing all five features, the eigenvalues of their correlation matrix are 3.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Standardizing was optional for PCA; the first two components explain 60 percent of the variance
Standardizing was needed, or income would dominate; the first two components explain 80 percent
Standardizing was needed, or income would dominate; the first component alone explains 80 percent
Standardizing should follow PCA, not precede it; the first two components explain 80 percent

explanation: PCA finds directions of maximum variance, so without standardizing, a feature with variance 10^8 would dominate the first component purely because of its units. After standardizing, the total variance equals the number of features, 3.0 + 1.0 + 0.5 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 5, so the first two components explain (3.0 + 1.0)/5 = 80 percent, and the first alone explains 3.0/5 = 60 percent. Standardizing is not optional when units differ this much, and it must happen before PCA to affect the components.

prompt: A t-SNE plot of customer embeddings shows three well-separated clusters, one large and two small, with the small ones far from the large one. A stakeholder concludes that the small clusters are very different from the large one and contain fewer customers. What should the data scientist say?

options.text: t-SNE cluster sizes and gaps are unreliable; check both claims in the original space
Both conclusions are reliable, because t-SNE preserves global distances between clusters
The plot is reliable only if it was produced with the default perplexity value
The small clusters are noise, because t-SNE always places outliers far from the main cluster

explanation: t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods but distorts global geometry: apparent cluster size and separation depend on perplexity and the optimization and do not reliably reflect true sizes or distances. Conclusions should be checked against the original data or with methods that preserve more global structure. t-SNE does not preserve global distances. No single perplexity makes global distances trustworthy. Small clusters are not automatically noise.

prompt: A team needs a 2-D embedding of 5 million records for visual exploration and also needs to project new records into the same embedding each day. Compared with t-SNE, which method fits better?

options.text: t-SNE, because it has a built-in transform that places new points without refitting
PCA to 2 components, because it preserves the non-linear neighbourhood structure
UMAP, which scales to large data sets and can transform new points with a fitted model
k-nearest neighbours, because it outputs a 2-D embedding of all of the records

explanation: UMAP is generally much faster than t-SNE on large data, tends to preserve more global structure, and a fitted UMAP model can embed new data. Standard t-SNE has no transform for new points and must be rerun. PCA is linear and does not preserve non-linear neighbourhoods. KNN is a prediction and search method, not an embedding technique.

prompt: A k-nearest neighbours classifier with k = 1 has 100 percent training accuracy but poor validation accuracy. What best explains this, and what should be tried?

options.text: k = 1 has high bias, since one neighbour is too few; use k = 0
KNN cannot overfit, because it has no parameters, so the validation set must be faulty
k = 1 underfits the training data, so the features should be scaled to fix the problem
k = 1 has high variance, since each point is its own neighbour; try a larger k

explanation: With k = 1, every training point is classified by itself, so training accuracy is trivially perfect, while predictions follow noise in individual points, which is high variance. Larger k averages over more neighbours and smooths the decision boundary; cross-validation can choose it. k = 1 is the low-bias extreme, and k = 0 is undefined. Non-parametric models can overfit badly. Perfect training accuracy is not underfitting.

prompt: A team wants to reduce a 2-million-document by 300,000-term TF-IDF matrix, stored in sparse format, to 200 dimensions for latent semantic analysis. Standard PCA would first centre the matrix. Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Standard PCA after converting the matrix to a dense array and centring it
t-SNE to 200 dimensions, because it preserves the topic structure of documents
Truncated singular value decomposition applied directly to the sparse matrix
k-means with k = 200, using the cluster labels as the 200 new dimensions

explanation: Truncated SVD computes only the top singular vectors and works directly on sparse matrices, which is the standard approach for latent semantic analysis. PCA's centring subtracts column means and makes the matrix dense, which for 2 million by 300,000 entries is far too large. t-SNE is designed for 2-D or 3-D visualization, not 200-dimensional reduction. Cluster labels are one categorical value per document, not 200 continuous dimensions.

prompt: A team plans to share a patient data set with researchers after removing names and record numbers. It still includes full date of birth, five-digit ZIP code and sex. What is the main privacy risk?

options.text: There is no risk, because names and record numbers were the only identifiers in the data set
The risk is only to data quality, because dates of birth are often entered with mistakes
Together these quasi-identifiers can re-identify many people, so generalize them
The risk applies only if the researchers are based abroad

explanation: Combinations of quasi-identifiers such as birth date, ZIP code and sex are unique for a large share of people and can be linked to public records, so removing direct identifiers is not enough. Generalizing (for example, birth year and a three-digit ZIP), suppression, or measures such as k-anonymity reduce the risk. Direct identifiers are not the only PII. The concern is privacy, not data quality. Re-identification risk exists wherever the researchers are located.

prompt: To protect customer emails in an analytics data set, an engineer replaces each email with its unsalted SHA-256 hash. The team calls the data anonymized. What is the problem?

options.text: It is only pseudonymization; known emails can be hashed and matched to re-identify
There is no problem, because SHA-256 hashes are mathematically impossible to reverse
SHA-256 should be replaced with MD5, because MD5 gives a stronger anonymization
Hashing changes the email length, which breaks downstream joins on the email field

explanation: Replacing an identifier with a consistent token is pseudonymization: anyone with a list of email addresses can hash them and match the results, so individuals remain identifiable, and regulations such as the GDPR treat pseudonymized data as personal data. Hash functions cannot be inverted directly, but dictionary matching does not need inversion. MD5 is weaker, not stronger. Consistent hashes actually keep joins working, which is part of why they remain linkable.

prompt: Developers need realistic customer data in a test environment to debug a billing application, but they must not see real names, card numbers or addresses. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Copying production data unchanged, with stricter passwords
Data masking that swaps sensitive fields for realistic, fictitious values
Encrypting the production data and sharing the decryption key with the developer team
Deleting every sensitive column, leaving the test database without those fields at all

explanation: Masking (a form of data obfuscation) replaces sensitive values with fictitious ones that keep formats and validation rules, so testing works without exposing real data. Copying production data exposes it regardless of password strength. Encryption with the key shared to developers gives them the real values. Dropping columns breaks the application logic that depends on those fields.

prompt: A company collected EU customers' addresses and purchase histories to process orders. The marketing team now wants to use the same data to train a model that targets promotions. Under the GDPR, what must be confirmed first?

options.text: That the new purpose is compatible or has its own lawful basis, such as consent
Nothing, because data the company already holds can be used for any internal purpose
Only that the model's accuracy meets the internal standard set for marketing models
Only that the data are stored on servers physically located inside the United States

explanation: The GDPR's purpose limitation principle requires personal data to be collected for specified purposes and not processed in ways incompatible with them; a new purpose needs a compatibility assessment or its own lawful basis, and data subjects must be informed. Holding data does not permit any use. Accuracy is irrelevant to lawfulness. Storing data in the United States does not satisfy purpose limitation and raises separate transfer rules.

prompt: A retention team proposes measuring a new churn-prevention program by the churn model's AUC. Leadership wants to know whether the program is working for the business. Which KPI is most appropriate?

options.text: Retention versus a randomized holdout group, with revenue retained
The churn model's AUC on the most recent month's validation data set
The number of retention offers sent to customers each month by the team
The number of features used by the churn model in its current version

explanation: A business KPI should measure the outcome the business cares about, here retention and revenue, and attribute it to the program by comparing with a holdout. AUC measures the model's ranking quality, not whether interventions retain customers. Offers sent is an activity measure that can rise while results fall. Feature count says nothing about value.

prompt: A proposed demand model would cost $200,000 a year to build and run. Analysis shows it would save about $150,000 a year in inventory costs. An improved spreadsheet rule would cost $20,000 a year and save about $90,000. What should the data scientist recommend?

options.text: The model, because its gross savings of $150,000 exceed the spreadsheet rule's savings
The model, because machine learning is the most appropriate solution for demand problems
The spreadsheet rule: a $70,000 net benefit versus a $50,000 net loss
Neither, because both cost money in the first year

explanation: A cost-benefit analysis compares net benefits: the model's $150,000 savings minus $200,000 cost is a $50,000 loss, while the rule's $90,000 minus $20,000 is a $70,000 gain. Translating the business need into the most appropriate solution sometimes means a simpler non-ML approach. Gross savings ignore cost. A method is not appropriate just because it is machine learning. Costs alone are not a reason to reject a solution with a positive net benefit.

prompt: A credit model was developed on applicants aged 21 to 65 with incomes from $20,000 to $200,000, all in one country. The business wants to use it unchanged for student applicants aged 18 to 20 in a new country. What is the main concern?

options.text: There is no concern, because a good model generalizes to any population of applicants
The applicants fall outside the model's relevant range of application
Only currency conversion, handled by rescaling incomes
The concern is training time, because new applicants require the model to be retrained

explanation: A model's relevant range of application is the population and conditions it was built and validated on; young students in a new country differ in age, income, credit history and regulation, so predictions are extrapolations that need validation, and possibly a new model. Generalization outside the training population cannot be assumed. Currency conversion does not address differences in behaviour or regulation. Training time is not the issue.

prompt: A partner shares proprietary sales data under an agreement that limits its use to a joint forecasting project. A product manager wants to use the same data to train a model for a separate product sold to other clients. What should the data scientist do?

options.text: Proceed, because data received from a partner belongs to the receiving company
Check the agreement and get the partner's written permission before any new use
Proceed after removing the partner's name from the data set so it cannot be traced
Proceed, because training a model is not the same as redistributing the original data

explanation: Proprietary data come with contractual restrictions, and using them outside the agreed purpose can breach the agreement even if the raw data are never shared. The agreement must be checked and permission obtained. Receiving data does not transfer ownership. Removing the partner's name does not change the contractual limits. Models trained on data can count as derived use under many agreements, so training is not automatically exempt.

prompt: A customer-satisfaction survey was emailed to all 20,000 customers, and 1,400 responded. The results show unusually high satisfaction. What is the main concern about this generated data?

options.text: Measurement drift: the survey instrument loses calibration as more responses arrive
Non-response bias: the 7 percent who replied may differ systematically from the rest
Sampling error only, which a sample of 1,400 responses makes negligible in practice
Granularity misalignment: survey answers are ordinal while customer records are numeric

explanation: Survey data are prone to self-selection: customers with strong feelings, often positive ones from loyal customers, are more likely to answer, so a 7 percent response rate can give a biased picture; weighting, follow-up of non-respondents or comparing respondent profiles helps. Instrument drift applies to sensors. A large sample reduces random error but not bias from who chose to respond. Mixing ordinal and numeric fields is not the main concern here.

prompt: A hospital readmission model uses diagnosis codes from administrative billing data. Readmission rates for one condition appear to jump in a single month. Investigation shows the hospital changed its coding guidelines that month. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Administrative data follow coding practices that can shift with no real-world change
Administrative data come from experiments, so the jump is real
Billing codes are sensor readings, so the jump reflects a calibration fault in the equipment
Administrative data are always more accurate than clinical data, so the jump is a real change

explanation: Administrative data are collected to run an operation, such as billing, not for analysis, so definitions and recording practices can shift for administrative reasons and create artificial changes. Understanding the data-generating process prevents misreading them. Administrative records are not experiments, not sensor readings, and are not inherently more accurate than clinical data.

prompt: A temperature sensor in a cold-storage unit has read about 1.5 degrees higher every month since installation, compared with a reference thermometer. Which characteristic of sensor data does this illustrate, and what should be done?

options.text: Random noise; average consecutive readings so that the deviation cancels out over time
Calibration drift; correct against the reference and schedule recalibration
Non-response bias; collect readings from more sensors so the average becomes accurate
Missing completely at random; impute the affected readings with the column mean

explanation: Sensor data can drift systematically as hardware ages; a growing offset against a reference is calibration drift, which needs correction and recalibration. Averaging removes random noise, not a consistent bias. Non-response bias applies to surveys. No readings are missing, so imputation does not apply.

prompt: An e-commerce company wants to model customers' interest in product categories. It has only transactional data, one row per completed purchase. What is the main limitation of this data source for the goal?

options.text: It contains too few rows, because transactional systems keep only monthly summaries
It is unstructured text, so it cannot be aggregated by customer or by category
It records only completed purchases, so browsing and abandoned interest are invisible
It is experimental data, so it cannot be used for any predictive modelling

explanation: Transactional data capture events that completed, such as purchases, payments or transfers, often in high volume and at fine granularity, but they say nothing about interest that did not convert, such as views or carts abandoned. Combining them with clickstream data would address the gap. Transaction tables are usually detailed rather than summarized. They are structured records, and they are observational rather than experimental.

prompt: A company wants to know whether free shipping causes higher order values. It can either analyse historical orders or run a test in which 50 percent of visitors are randomly offered free shipping. Why is the experimental data preferable?

options.text: Experimental data are always larger than historical data, giving more statistical power
Experimental data never have missing values to clean
Historical order data cannot be joined to shipping information in a relational database
Random assignment makes groups comparable, so differences reflect the offer

explanation: In experimental data the analyst controls assignment, and randomization balances confounders such as customer type or season, supporting a causal conclusion. Historical data reflect who happened to get free shipping, which may be confounded. Experiments are often smaller than historical data. They can still have missing values. Joining historical data is a technical matter, not the reason for preferring experiments.

prompt: A help-desk data set records time_to_resolution only for tickets that have been closed. An analyst computes the average resolution time from this field to report current performance. Why is understanding the data-generating process important here?

options.text: Open tickets, often the slowest, are excluded, so the average understates resolution time
Closed tickets are generated by sensors, so their times include calibration error
The field is generated randomly by the system, so its average has no meaning
The data-generating process matters only for synthetic data, not for operational data

explanation: Knowing how and when a value is recorded reveals that unresolved tickets are absent, a form of censoring that biases the average downward, especially when the backlog contains hard cases; survival methods or reporting the open backlog alongside gives a truer picture. Ticket times come from system timestamps, not sensors with calibration error, and are not random. The data-generating process matters for every data source.

prompt: A bank plans to create a synthetic version of its customer transaction data so that an external vendor can build models without seeing real records. Which process is most appropriate?

options.text: Copy the real records and change each customer's name to a randomly generated one
Generate every column independently from a uniform distribution over its observed range
Fit a generative model to the real data, sample from it, then check fidelity and privacy
Shuffle each column separately, then send the shuffled real values to the vendor

explanation: A sound synthetic data process models the joint distribution of the real data, samples new records, then validates both fidelity (statistical properties and model utility) and privacy (for example, that no synthetic record closely reproduces a real one). Renaming customers leaves real transaction values linkable. Independent uniform columns destroy the relationships the vendor needs. Shuffling columns keeps real values and breaks correlations.

prompt: A fraud team trained a model entirely on synthetic transactions generated from a model of last year's data. It performs well on synthetic test data but poorly on a new fraud scheme in production. Which limitation of synthetic data does this show?

options.text: Synthetic data always contain personal data, so the model cannot be used in production
Synthetic data reproduce only the patterns the generator learned, not genuinely new ones
Synthetic data are too large to train on, so the model was undertrained for production
Synthetic data have no class imbalance, so fraud becomes far too common in training

explanation: A generator can only produce variations of the structure it learned from its source data, so new behaviour, such as a novel fraud scheme, and rare patterns the generator smoothed over are missing; validation on real, current data is essential. Synthetic data can be created to protect privacy, not necessarily containing personal data. Size was not the problem. Class balance in synthetic data depends on how it was generated.

prompt: A team testing a new data pipeline needs thousands of records with edge cases such as leap-day dates, empty strings, maximum-length names and extreme amounts, which are rare in production. What is the main rationale for using synthetic data here?

options.text: It always reproduces the exact statistical distribution of the production data
It removes the need for any testing with production-like volumes and formats
It can include rare edge cases in any quantity without exposing real data
It is the only legal way to test a pipeline that processes financial records

explanation: Synthetic data let a team design the sample itself, oversampling rare edge cases to exercise every code path, while avoiding the privacy risk of copying real records. Synthetic data do not automatically match production distributions exactly; here the aim is deliberately different. They complement, not replace, realistic volume and format testing. Other options, such as masked data, can also be lawful.

prompt: A team wants to buy a commercial data set of business firmographics to enrich a lead-scoring model. The vendor's licence allows internal analytics only. The product team wants to show the purchased fields to clients in the company's software. What should the data scientist do?

options.text: Proceed, because purchased data become the buyer's property to use in any way
Flag the licence conflict and get legal review or a broader licence first
Proceed, because showing data inside software is not the same as redistribution
Proceed after renaming the purchased fields so the vendor cannot recognise them

explanation: Commercial data come with licensing terms that restrict how they can be used, and exposing licensed fields to clients usually counts as redistribution beyond internal analytics, so the licence must be reviewed and expanded if needed. Buying a licence does not transfer ownership. Displaying data to outside users is a form of distribution. Renaming fields does not change the licence obligations.

prompt: A start-up wants to use a public image data set released under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial licence to train a model for a paid product. What is the main issue?

options.text: The NonCommercial term bars commercial use without the licensor's permission
No issue, because public data can be used for any purpose
The only requirement is to credit the creators somewhere in the product's documentation
The licence allows commercial use as long as the trained model is not shared publicly

explanation: Public availability does not mean unrestricted use; a Creative Commons NonCommercial licence prohibits use primarily intended for commercial advantage, so using the data for a paid product needs permission or alternative data, with legal review. Attribution alone satisfies only the attribution part of the licence. Keeping the model private does not make the use non-commercial.

prompt: Analysts query a 2 TB table with 200 columns but typically read only 3 or 4 columns and filter by date. The data are currently stored as CSV files. Which format change would most reduce the data scanned?

options.text: JSON, a self-describing format that stores the field names alongside every value
Parquet, a columnar format that reads only the needed columns and skips row groups
Uncompressed CSV with a header row, so column names are easier to locate
Tab-separated values, which can be read faster than comma-separated values

explanation: Parquet stores data by column with embedded statistics and compression, so queries read only the referenced columns and can skip row groups whose date range does not match. JSON repeats field names in every record and must be parsed row by row, increasing size. CSV and TSV are row-oriented text formats, so every query reads every column regardless of headers or delimiters.

prompt: Classify the storage type for each source: (1) customer orders in relational tables with a fixed schema; (2) application events in JSON with nested fields that vary by event type; (3) recorded support calls as audio files.

options.text: (1) Structured, (2) semi-structured, (3) unstructured
(1) Structured, (2) unstructured, (3) semi-structured
(1) Semi-structured, (2) structured, (3) unstructured
(1) Structured, (2) structured, (3) semi-structured

explanation: Relational tables with a fixed schema are structured data. JSON events carry their own field names and allow nested, variable structure, which makes them semi-structured. Audio files have no inherent field structure and are unstructured, typically kept in object storage with separate metadata. The other options mislabel at least one source; for example, JSON is not unstructured, because it has tags and keys that give it structure.

prompt: A distributed processing job reads one 300 GB gzip-compressed CSV file and runs on a single worker while the rest of the cluster sits idle. What is the most likely cause, and what is a better approach?

options.text: The cluster has too few workers; add more nodes so that the gzip file is read faster
CSV cannot be compressed safely; decompress it and store the 300 GB as plain JSON
The file is too small for a cluster; process it locally on a laptop instead
Gzip files cannot be split for parallel reads; use a splittable format such as Parquet

explanation: A single gzip stream must be decompressed from the start, so a framework cannot split it among workers, and one worker reads the whole file. Storing the data in a splittable columnar format such as Parquet (with internal block compression), or as many smaller files, allows parallel processing. Adding nodes does not help when the file cannot be split. JSON would be larger and still need splitting. At 300 GB the data are too big for comfortable single-machine processing.

prompt: A data set has 100 million rows and 50 numeric columns stored as 64-bit floating-point values. Roughly how much memory is needed to hold it in memory as a dense array, before any overhead?

options.text: About 4 GB
About 40 GB
About 400 GB
About 5 GB

explanation: Memory is rows x columns x bytes per value: 100,000,000 x 50 x 8 bytes = 40,000,000,000 bytes, about 40 GB. This sizing tells whether the data fit in one machine's memory or need chunked, out-of-core or distributed processing. The figure 4 GB is off by a factor of 10, and 400 GB by a factor of 10 the other way. About 5 GB is the result of using 1 byte per value instead of 8.

prompt: A team will train a large convolutional neural network on millions of images. Which hardware is most appropriate, and why?

options.text: High-clock-speed CPUs, because deep learning work is mostly sequential branching logic
Large-capacity hard drives, because training speed depends mainly on storage capacity
A single CPU core, because neural network training cannot be parallelized at all
GPUs or TPUs, which run deep learning's parallel matrix operations efficiently

explanation: Training neural networks is dominated by large matrix multiplications and convolutions that parallelize across thousands of simple cores; GPUs and Google's TPUs are built for exactly this, often training many times faster than CPUs. Deep learning is not mostly sequential branching. Storage capacity matters for holding data but does not drive compute speed. Training parallelizes very well.

prompt: A card issuer must score each transaction for fraud before authorization, within 200 ms. Its finance team also needs a daily summary report each morning. Which ingestion approaches fit these two needs?

options.text: Batch processing every night for fraud scoring and streaming for the daily report
Batch processing every hour for both fraud scoring and the daily report
Streaming ingestion for fraud scoring and batch processing for the daily report
Streaming for both, because batch processing is obsolete for financial data

explanation: Streaming processes each event as it arrives, which is required to score a transaction within 200 ms. A daily report tolerates latency and benefits from batch processing's efficiency and simplicity, on a daily refresh cycle. Nightly or hourly batches are far too slow for authorization-time scoring. Batch processing remains appropriate and cost-effective for periodic reporting.

prompt: A nightly pipeline extracts data, builds features and retrains a model. Steps must run in order, failed steps should retry automatically, and on-call staff need alerts and run history. Which approach fits best?

options.text: A set of independent scheduled scripts that each start at a fixed clock time
A data scientist who runs each notebook by hand every night and checks the output
A single long script with no retries, so that any failure stops the pipeline at once
A workflow orchestration tool that defines the steps as a DAG with retries and alerts

explanation: Orchestration tools model a pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of tasks with explicit dependencies, scheduling, retries, alerting and run history, which automates the pipeline reliably. Fixed-time scripts do not enforce dependencies and break when an upstream step is late. Manual runs do not scale and are error-prone. A monolithic script without retries makes transient failures fatal and gives poor visibility.

prompt: A daily pipeline appends the day's sales to a target table. When a failed run was retried, the day's sales were loaded twice, doubling the totals. Which design principle would prevent this?

options.text: Increase the number of retries so that the pipeline is more likely to succeed
Run the pipeline less often so that failures and retries happen less frequently
Make the load idempotent, such as overwriting the day's partition each run
Store the target table in CSV format instead of a columnar format like Parquet

explanation: An idempotent pipeline step produces the same result whether it runs once or several times, for example by replacing the partition for the processing date or by merging on a unique key instead of blindly appending. More retries make duplication more likely. Running less often does not remove the duplication risk. File format does not affect whether appends are duplicated.

prompt: Transaction data older than two years are rarely queried but must be kept for seven years for regulatory reasons. Active storage costs are rising. What should the team do?

options.text: Delete data older than two years, because it is rarely queried by analysts
Archive older data to cold storage under a seven-year retention policy
Keep all seven years in the fastest storage tier so that queries stay quick
Move the older data to analysts' laptops, where storage is effectively free

explanation: Archiving moves infrequently used data to cheaper storage tiers while it persists and can be retrieved, and a retention policy ensures it is kept for the required seven years and then deleted. Deleting it breaches the retention requirement. Keeping everything in the fastest tier wastes money on rarely used data. Laptops are insecure, unreliable and unmanaged.

prompt: A regulator asks a bank to show exactly which source systems, transformations and versions of data were used to produce the training set for a credit model. Which capability answers this?

options.text: A data dictionary that defines each column that appears in the training set
A larger set of unit tests for each function in the feature engineering code
Data lineage tracking from sources through each transformation to the training set
Streaming ingestion, so that the training data are always as recent as possible

explanation: Data lineage records where data came from and every transformation applied along the way, so a team can trace a training set back to its sources and versions, which supports audits and debugging. A data dictionary defines fields, not their origin and processing history. Unit tests check code correctness. Ingestion mode does not record provenance.

prompt: A customers table has 10,000 rows and an orders table has 25,000 rows. 1,500 customers have no orders. The analyst needs a row for every customer, including those without orders, with order details where they exist. Which join should be used?

options.text: An inner join between customers and orders on customer_id
A left join from customers to orders on customer_id
A right join from customers to orders on customer_id
A cross join between the customers and orders tables

explanation: A left join keeps every row of the left table (customers) and adds matching order rows, filling order fields with nulls for the 1,500 customers without orders. An inner join drops customers with no orders. A right join from customers to orders keeps all orders and only the customers who have them. A cross join pairs every customer with every order, producing 250 million meaningless rows.

prompt: An analyst joins a 1,000-row customers table to an addresses table on customer_id and gets 1,350 rows instead of 1,000. Row counts were logged before and after the step. What is the most likely cause and the correct response?

options.text: The join type was wrong; switching to an inner join always restores 1,000 rows
The logging was wrong, because a join can never return more rows than its inputs
Duplicate customers exist in the customers table; delete 350 of them at random
customer_id repeats in addresses; fix the key or keep one address per customer

explanation: When the key on the right side is not unique, each customer matches several addresses and the join fans out; tracking observation counts at each step reveals this. The fix is to define the right key or deduplicate, for example by choosing the current address. An inner join fans out in the same way. Joins can return more rows than either input when keys repeat. Deleting random customers destroys valid data.

prompt: A team matches 50,000 supplier names from an invoice system to a vendor master list. Exact matching on name links only 72 percent of records, because of typos, abbreviations and punctuation. What is the best approach?

options.text: Normalize names, fuzzy join on string similarity, and review borderline matches
Accept the 72 percent match rate, because unmatched records are probably invalid
Match on the first three letters of each name to raise the match rate quickly
Use a cross join and keep the pair with the most characters in common for each name

explanation: Standardizing case, punctuation and common abbreviations, then fuzzy matching on a similarity measure such as edit distance with a threshold, raises the match rate, and reviewing borderline scores controls false matches. Unmatched records are usually valid suppliers with formatting differences. Three-letter prefixes create many false matches. A cross join of 50,000 names against the master list is very costly, and raw character overlap is a crude score.

prompt: An analyst has two monthly customer extracts with identical columns and wants (1) one table containing every customer who appears in either month, with no duplicates, and (2) a list of customers present in both months. Which operations should be used?

options.text: (1) An intersection; (2) a union with deduplication
(1) A union with deduplication; (2) an intersection
(1) A union that keeps duplicates; (2) a left join
(1) A cross join; (2) a union with deduplication

explanation: A union stacks the rows of tables with the same schema; deduplicating (UNION rather than UNION ALL in SQL) leaves each customer once. An intersection returns only rows present in both inputs. Swapping them reverses the meaning. A union that keeps duplicates lists customers twice, and a left join returns all customers from the first month. A cross join pairs every row with every other row.

prompt: Event timestamps arrive from three systems in different forms: 03/04/2024 14:05 in local US time, 2024-04-03T18:05:00Z, and Unix epoch seconds. The analyst needs to order events across systems. What should be done?

options.text: Sort the timestamps as text strings, because every format contains the date and time
Drop the time zones and treat every timestamp as local time to keep things simple
Keep only the date part of each timestamp, since times differ between systems
Parse each format explicitly and convert all timestamps to UTC in one standard format

explanation: Date and time standardization requires parsing each source's format explicitly (03/04/2024 is ambiguous between March 4 and April 3 unless the source convention is known), converting to a common time zone such as UTC and storing in a standard representation such as ISO 8601. Text sorting orders strings, not instants. Ignoring time zones misorders events by hours. Dropping times loses the ordering within each day.

prompt: Which regular expression matches a complete US ZIP code in either 5-digit form (12345) or ZIP+4 form (12345-6789), and nothing else?
explanation: The pattern anchors the start (^) and end ($), requires exactly five digits, and makes the group of a hyphen plus four digits optional with ?. Without the optional group, the pattern rejects plain 5-digit ZIP codes. Without anchors, the pattern also matches five digits inside longer strings such as 1234567. The range of 4 to 9 digits accepts invalid lengths and rejects the hyphenated form.

prompt: In a patient table, age is recorded as 999 when unknown. The analyst reports a mean age of 87 for a clinic whose patients are mostly in their forties. What is the problem and the fix?

options.text: The clinic's patients are older than expected; report the mean of 87 as correct
The missing code 999 is treated as a real age; recode it to null before analysis
Ages above 100 are outliers; winsorize all ages at the 95th percentile instead
The age field is categorical; compute the mode of the field rather than the mean

explanation: Sentinel values such as 999 or -1 are missing codes, and treating them as data inflates the mean; they should be recoded to null and handled with an appropriate missing-data method. The data, not the patients, explain the result. Winsorizing would turn 999 into a large but still false age. Age is numeric, and switching to the mode hides rather than fixes the missing code.

prompt: Patient weights from five clinics are being combined. One clinic's mean weight is about 2.2 times the others', and its staff confirm they record weight in pounds while the rest use kilograms. How should this error be classified and fixed?

options.text: A systematic error; convert that clinic's values to kilograms before combining
An idiosyncratic error; delete that clinic's records as random data entry noise
A valid difference; that clinic's patients are simply heavier than average
An idiosyncratic error; winsorize that clinic's weights at the 99th percentile

explanation: A systematic error affects many records in the same way for a consistent reason, here a unit difference, and is fixed by unit conversion and standardization (divide pounds by about 2.205). Idiosyncratic errors are one-off mistakes such as individual typos, without a consistent pattern. A uniform 2.2 ratio is the pound-to-kilogram factor, not real weight differences. Deleting or winsorizing discards or distorts recoverable data.

prompt: Household income has extreme values, a few in the tens of millions, that are verified as genuine. They dominate a linear model. The analyst winsorizes at the 1st and 99th percentiles, which are $8,000 and $410,000. What happens to a verified income of $12 million?

options.text: It is deleted, because winsorizing removes values beyond the cut points
It is set to $410,000, keeping the record while limiting its influence
It is set to the median income, because winsorizing replaces outliers with the center
It is unchanged, because winsorizing applies only to values judged to be errors

explanation: Winsorization caps values beyond chosen cut points at those cut points, so $12 million becomes $410,000; the record stays in the data with reduced leverage. Here the value is valid, not an error, so capping (or a robust model or log transform) is preferable to deletion. Deleting is trimming, not winsorizing. Replacement with the median is a different imputation approach. Winsorizing applies to extreme values regardless of whether they are errors.

prompt: An API returns orders as JSON, each with order_id, customer and an items array of objects with sku and quantity. The analyst needs a table with one row per item for analysis. What should be done?

options.text: Keep one row per order and store the items array as a single text column
Keep only the first item in each order, so each order maps to a single row
Flatten the JSON: one row per item, repeating the order-level fields
Create a separate column for each possible item position, up to the largest order

explanation: Data flattening turns nested structures into tabular form; exploding the array gives one row per item, with order_id and customer repeated so each row is self-contained and can be aggregated. A text column hides the item data from analysis. Keeping only the first item loses data. One column per item position creates a wide, sparse table that is awkward to analyse and breaks when larger orders appear.

prompt: A data set has 15 percent missing values in several correlated predictors. Single mean imputation made confidence intervals look unrealistically narrow. Which imputation approach better reflects uncertainty?

options.text: Mean imputation followed by doubling all of the reported standard errors
Replacing every missing value with zero, because zero is a neutral number
Multiple imputation, pooling results across several imputed data sets
Deleting every row with any missing value and keeping the narrower intervals

explanation: Single mean imputation treats filled-in values as known, shrinking variance and correlations and understating uncertainty. Multiple imputation creates several plausible completed data sets by modelling each variable from the others, analyses each, and pools results so that the extra uncertainty from missingness appears in the standard errors. Doubling standard errors is arbitrary. Zero is not neutral and biases results. Listwise deletion loses data and can bias results unless data are missing completely at random.

prompt: Three annotators label customer emails as complaint or not complaint for a training set. Their agreement is low for a large share of emails. What should the team do to improve ground truth quality?

options.text: Use the first annotator's labels only, because a single labeller is always consistent
Refine the guidelines, measure agreement with kappa, and adjudicate disputes
Drop every email on which the annotators disagree, keeping only unanimous labels
Let the model decide the disputed labels and add its predictions to the training set

explanation: Ground truth labels depend on clear guidelines, and inter-annotator agreement statistics such as Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa quantify reliability; disagreements should be adjudicated by an expert and used to sharpen the guidelines. A single annotator is not automatically consistent or correct. Dropping all disputed cases biases the data toward easy examples. Using the model's predictions as labels reinforces its own errors.

prompt: A project following CRISP-DM reaches the evaluation phase. The model meets its technical metrics but would not achieve the business objective agreed at the start. What should happen next?

options.text: Proceed to deployment, because the model has met all of its technical metrics
Skip back to data preparation only, because evaluation never affects the objective
End the project, because CRISP-DM allows only one pass through each phase
Return to business understanding to revisit the objective, data and approach

explanation: CRISP-DM's six phases are business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment, and the process is iterative. The evaluation phase checks results against the business objectives, and a failure there usually sends the team back to business understanding to reassess goals, success criteria and approach. Deploying a model that misses the objective wastes effort. Data preparation alone may not address a mismatch in objectives. CRISP-DM explicitly allows iteration.

prompt: A company wants a vendor-neutral reference framework covering data governance, data quality, metadata management, data architecture and data security across the organization. Which framework is designed for this?

options.text: CRISP-DM, the data mining process model
Scrum, the iterative framework for delivering software in sprints
The DAMA Data Management Body of Knowledge (DAMA-DMBOK)
The Agile Manifesto, the statement of values for software teams

explanation: DAMA-DMBOK, published by the Data Management Association, describes data management knowledge areas such as governance, data quality, metadata, architecture and security, making it a reference for organization-wide data management. CRISP-DM is a life-cycle model for individual data mining projects. Scrum and the Agile Manifesto guide how teams deliver work, not what data management functions to establish.

prompt: A team versions its code in Git but cannot tell which version of a 200 GB training data set produced last quarter's model. Committing the data directly to Git is impractical. What should they do?

options.text: Version the data as immutable snapshots referenced from each Git commit
Commit the 200 GB data set into the Git repository alongside the training code
Keep one copy of the data set and overwrite it in place whenever new data arrive
Record the date of each training run in the commit message and rely on that

explanation: Data version control tools and immutable, hashed snapshots in object storage record exactly which data were used, with only a small pointer or hash stored in Git, so each model can be traced to both its code and its data. Large binary files bloat Git repositories and slow every clone. Overwriting data in place destroys history. A date does not identify the data's contents if data were modified on that day.

prompt: Production is serving a model, and the team must be able to reproduce it, roll back to the previous version, and know the hyperparameters used for each version. Which practice provides this?

options.text: A model registry versioning each model with its hyperparameters and code commit
Saving each model file as model_final.pkl, overwriting the previous one on each run
Storing hyperparameters only in the data scientist's notebook from the last training run
Retraining a fresh model from scratch whenever a rollback becomes necessary

explanation: Versioning models together with their hyperparameters, metrics and code and data versions, typically in a model registry, enables reproduction, auditing and quick rollback to a known-good version. Overwriting a single file erases history. Notebook-only records are easily lost and are not linked to deployed artefacts. Retraining for a rollback is slow and may not reproduce the previous model exactly.

prompt: A data scientist is turning a 2,000-line exploratory notebook into a reusable package with modules, tests and debugging. Which tool feature set is most useful for this work?

options.text: A notebook environment with every cell merged into one very large cell
A plain text editor with no syntax highlighting, to avoid distractions
An IDE with debugging, refactoring, linting, testing and Git integration
A spreadsheet application, so that intermediate results can be inspected

explanation: Integrated development environments provide debugging, code navigation, refactoring, linting, integrated testing and version control, which suit restructuring code into a maintainable package. Notebooks are good for exploration, but merging cells makes debugging harder. A plain editor lacks the tools needed for safe refactoring. Spreadsheets are not code development tools.

prompt: A company plans to distribute a commercial desktop application that bundles an open-source library licensed under the GNU GPL version 3. The company does not want to release its own source code. What is the main concern?

options.text: No concern, because open-source code has no conditions
The only concern is crediting the library's authors in the application's About box
GPL code may be used only by non-profit organizations, so the company cannot use it
GPL copyleft terms can require releasing the combined work's source code

explanation: The GPL is a copyleft licence: distributing a work that incorporates GPL code generally requires licensing the combined work under the GPL and providing its source, which conflicts with keeping the company's code closed. Dependency licences should be reviewed, often with legal advice, and permissive licences such as MIT or Apache 2.0 considered. Open-source licences do have conditions. Attribution alone is the requirement of permissive licences, not copyleft ones. The GPL does not restrict use to non-profits.

prompt: A team retrieves data from a third-party REST API that returns 100 records per page and allows 60 requests per minute. Their script requests only the first page and sometimes receives HTTP 429 errors. What should they change?

options.text: Request the first page repeatedly in parallel threads to obtain the rest of the data faster
Ignore the HTTP 429 responses, because they indicate a problem with the API provider
Follow the pagination links and back off and retry when rate-limited, honouring the limits
Switch from HTTPS to HTTP, which removes rate limits from most REST APIs

explanation: APIs often split large results across pages, so a client must follow the next-page token or link until no pages remain. HTTP 429 means too many requests, so the client should wait (for example, exponential backoff, honouring any Retry-After header) and stay within 60 requests a minute. Parallel requests worsen rate limiting and repeat the same page. Ignoring 429 errors loses data. The transport protocol does not remove rate limits.

prompt: A model is exposed as a REST endpoint used by several applications. A new model version expects an additional input field. What is the best practice for the endpoint?

options.text: Replace the model behind the current endpoint immediately and let failing clients adapt
Accept any input without validation and fill missing fields with zeros automatically
Add a new versioned endpoint with input validation and keep the old one for now
Ask every client team to call the model's Python code directly instead of the API

explanation: Model services should have a defined, validated input schema and versioning, so that changes do not break existing clients and old versions can be retired after migration. Swapping the model in place breaks clients that do not send the new field. Silently filling missing fields with zeros produces wrong predictions without any error. Calling code directly removes the benefits of a service, such as isolation, scaling and monitoring.

prompt: Which statement best describes the different roles of docstrings and inline comments in Python data science code?

options.text: Docstrings document what a function does, its parameters and returns; comments explain why
Docstrings explain why individual lines exist; comments list each function's parameters
Docstrings and comments are interchangeable, so a function needs only one of the two
Docstrings are needed only for private functions; public functions should use comments

explanation: A docstring is the first string in a module, class or function and documents its purpose, parameters, return values and exceptions, and tools can read it for help and generated documentation. Inline comments should explain non-obvious reasoning, such as why a threshold was chosen, rather than restate the code. The roles are not reversed or interchangeable. Public interfaces especially need docstrings. Markdown, such as README files and notebook text cells, documents the project and process at a higher level.

prompt: A feature function is 300 lines long, uses unexplained constants such as 0.37 and 14, and repeats the same date-parsing block four times. Which clean code change is most appropriate?

options.text: Split it into small named functions, name the constants, and remove repetition
Add a comment above each of the 300 lines explaining what that line does
Rename the function to something shorter so the long body is easier to call
Combine the function with the other feature functions into one larger function

explanation: Clean code practices favour small functions with a single responsibility and descriptive names, named constants instead of magic numbers, and removing duplication (don't repeat yourself), which makes code easier to test and maintain. Commenting every line adds noise without fixing the structure. Renaming does not address length or duplication. Merging functions makes the problem worse.

prompt: A function normalize_amount(x) converts transaction amounts in various string formats, such as $1,200.50, (45.00) for negatives and blanks, into floats. Which unit tests are most valuable to write?

options.text: A single test confirming that the function runs without error on one typical amount
Tests that check only the function's speed on one million randomly generated amounts
Tests of known inputs and outputs, including blanks, negatives and malformed text
No tests, because the function will be checked when the full pipeline is run

explanation: Unit tests should check a small unit of code against known expected outputs, especially edge cases such as blanks, parenthesized negatives, thousands separators and malformed values, so that regressions are caught immediately. A single happy-path test misses the risky cases. Performance tests do not verify correctness. Relying on full pipeline runs makes failures late, slow to diagnose and easy to miss.

prompt: A team retrains a model weekly. Twice, a retrained model with a bug in feature code reached production. Which change best prevents this?

options.text: Retraining the model daily, so that any bug is replaced with a new model more quickly
A CI/CD pipeline that runs unit tests and validation gates before any model is deployed
Deploying every retrained model directly to production and checking dashboards later
Moving the training code into a single notebook so that it is easier to read

explanation: Continuous integration runs automated tests on every code change, and continuous delivery or deployment promotes a model only after it passes validation gates, such as metric thresholds against the current model and data checks, so buggy versions are stopped. Retraining more often just ships bugs more often. Deploying without gates lets errors reach users. A notebook does not add testing or gating.

prompt: A model service must scale from 3 to 40 replicas during daily traffic peaks, replace failed instances automatically, and roll out new versions with no downtime. Which technology addresses these needs?

options.text: A single large virtual machine sized for the peak load
A container orchestration platform such as Kubernetes
A cron job that restarts the service script every hour
A shared network drive holding the model file for all users

explanation: Container orchestration platforms schedule containers across nodes, scale replicas with load, restart or replace failed containers, and support rolling updates without downtime. A single large VM cannot scale horizontally or survive its own failure and wastes capacity off-peak. Hourly restarts do not scale or heal failures. A shared drive stores files but does not run or manage services.

prompt: A team compares running each model service in its own virtual machine with running it in a container. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Containers include a full guest OS on a hypervisor; VMs share the host operating system kernel
VMs and containers are identical, because both are just different names for virtualization
VMs include a full guest OS on a hypervisor; containers share the host kernel and start faster
Containers cannot run on cloud platforms, so VMs are required for every cloud deployment

explanation: Virtualization uses a hypervisor to run complete guest operating systems, giving strong isolation at the cost of more overhead and slower startup. Containers package an application and its dependencies but share the host OS kernel, so they are lighter and start in seconds. The reversed statement swaps the two. They are different technologies. Containers run widely on cloud platforms.

prompt: Two projects on the same server need different versions of the same Python library, and upgrading it for one project breaks the other. What is the best solution?

options.text: Install both library versions globally and let Python choose one at random at runtime
Keep the older library version for both projects and never upgrade any dependency again
Copy the library's source code into each project's folder and edit it until both work
Isolate each project in its own virtual environment or container with pinned dependencies

explanation: Code isolation with per-project virtual environments or containers gives each project its own dependency set, and pinning versions in a lock or requirements file makes environments reproducible. A global installation can hold only one active version of a package. Never upgrading leaves security and compatibility problems. Editing copied library code creates an unmaintainable fork.

prompt: Data scientists run heavy training queries against the production transactional database, slowing the customer-facing application. Which approach best addresses this?

options.text: Run the training queries during business hours, when more database staff are available
Give the data scientists administrator access so their queries get higher priority
Reduce the application's connection limit so that the training queries can complete
Replicate the data to a read replica or analytics store and point training queries there

explanation: Data replication copies production data to a separate replica or analytics store, isolating analytical workloads from transactional ones while keeping data current; replicas also provide redundancy. Running queries during business hours makes the impact worse. Administrator access gives more power, not less load. Starving the application of connections harms customers.

prompt: A loan default model is in production, but true default labels arrive only after 12 months. How can the team monitor model performance in the meantime?

options.text: Monitor input drift and score distributions, then accuracy as labels arrive
Wait 12 months before doing any monitoring, because there is nothing to measure
Measure accuracy daily by treating each prediction as its own ground truth label
Retrain the model every day so that monitoring becomes unnecessary in practice

explanation: When labels are delayed, proxies such as shifts in input distributions (for example, with population stability or KS statistics), changes in score distributions and data-quality checks provide early warning, and performance metrics are computed once outcomes mature. Waiting a year leaves problems undetected. Comparing predictions with themselves always gives perfect accuracy. Frequent retraining without monitoring can silently deploy worse models.

prompt: A new recommendation model beats the current model on offline holdout metrics. Before full rollout, the team wants to confirm its effect on real user behaviour. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the offline holdout evaluation with a different random seed and compare
Online validation, such as an A/B test routing a share of live traffic to the new model
Deploy the new model to all users at once and compare this month's revenue with last month's
Ask the data science team to rate a sample of recommendations from each model

explanation: Offline validation uses historical data and cannot capture feedback effects, such as how users respond to different recommendations. Online validation, such as an A/B test with randomized traffic splitting, measures real impact and can be stopped if harm appears. Another offline run gives the same kind of evidence. A before-and-after comparison is confounded by time. Internal ratings do not measure user behaviour.

prompt: A team wants to deploy a new fraud model without affecting customers at first. It plans to send every live transaction to both the current and the new model, act only on the current model's decisions, and compare outputs. What is this deployment pattern?

options.text: A/B testing, in which half of the customers are served by each of the two models
Shadow deployment, in which the new model scores live traffic silently
Blue-green deployment, switching all traffic at once
Batch scoring, in which the new model scores last month's transactions overnight

explanation: In shadow mode the new model receives real production inputs and its predictions are logged and compared, but they do not influence outcomes, which validates behaviour and latency safely before a live A/B test or rollout. A/B testing lets the new model's decisions affect a share of users. Blue-green deployment switches traffic between two environments. Batch scoring of historical data is offline, not live.

prompt: A factory needs a vision model to reject defective parts on a production line within 20 ms. The site's internet connection is unreliable. Which deployment environment fits best?

options.text: Edge deployment on a device or gateway located at the production line
Cloud deployment in a distant region with automatic scaling
A hybrid setup in which every image is sent to the cloud for scoring
Cluster deployment in the company's head-office data centre

explanation: Edge deployment runs inference next to the data source, avoiding network round-trips and keeping the line working when connectivity drops, which suits strict latency and unreliable links. Sending images to the cloud or to a remote data centre adds network latency and fails when the connection is down, whatever the scaling or hardware.

prompt: A defence contractor must keep all data and models inside its own facilities under contract rules, and already owns suitable GPU servers. Which deployment environment fits best?

options.text: Public cloud deployment with data encrypted at rest
On-premises deployment on the contractor's own servers
Edge deployment on employees' personal mobile devices
Hybrid deployment that bursts training to a public cloud

explanation: On-premises deployment keeps data and models within the organization's own facilities and control, satisfying the contractual requirement and using hardware it already owns. Encryption does not change the fact that public cloud infrastructure is outside the contractor's facilities. Personal devices are neither controlled facilities nor suitable for this workload. Bursting to the public cloud moves data outside the facilities.

prompt: A hospital must keep identifiable patient records on premises, but occasionally needs large GPU capacity to train models on de-identified data. Which deployment approach fits best?

options.text: Fully on-premises deployment, buying enough GPUs for the rare peak training jobs
